title: Perfect competition
overview: Perfect competition is the theoretical benchmark against which every other market structure is judged. Firms are price takers, so the model shows how free entry and exit drive price down to the minimum of average cost, producing normal profit and both allocative and productive efficiency in the long run. Edexcel expects you to draw the short-run and long-run diagrams accurately and to evaluate how useful an unrealistic model is.
objectives: State and explain the characteristics of a perfectly competitive market
Explain why the firm is a price taker and why AR = MR = P is horizontal
Draw and explain short-run supernormal profit and loss for a perfectly competitive firm, including the shutdown condition
Use linked industry and firm diagrams to explain the movement to long-run equilibrium
Show why long-run equilibrium is allocatively and productively efficient, and evaluate dynamic efficiency
Evaluate the realism and usefulness of the model using real markets

sections.heading: Characteristics of perfect competition
sections.body:
Perfect competition is a market structure defined by a set of assumptions. Each one matters because it drives a specific result in the model.

- **Many buyers and sellers**: each firm is tiny relative to the market, so no single firm can influence the market price by changing its own output.
- **Homogeneous (identical) products**: consumers see the output of one firm as a perfect substitute for any other, so there is no brand loyalty and no reason to pay more to one seller.
- **Perfect information**: buyers and sellers know all prices and all technology. Any firm charging above the market price loses every customer instantly, and no firm has a secret cost advantage.
- **Freedom of entry and exit**: there are no barriers. Firms can enter when supernormal profit exists and leave when losses are made, with no sunk costs.
- **Firms are profit maximisers**: they produce where MC = MR.

Together these make each firm a **price taker**. The price is set by market demand and supply, and the individual firm can sell as much as it likes at that price but nothing above it. If it charged slightly more, demand for its output would fall to zero because identical products are available elsewhere and everyone knows it. There is also no reason to charge less, since it can already sell everything at the market price.

No real market meets all of these conditions. The closest approximations are markets for agricultural commodities (wheat, potatoes sold at wholesale), some financial markets such as foreign exchange, and online marketplaces for standardised products where price comparison is instant. The value of the model is as a benchmark: it shows what competition can achieve at its most extreme.

sections.heading: The price-taking firm: AR = MR = P
sections.body:
Because the firm can sell any quantity at the market price, every extra unit adds exactly the price to total revenue. So for the perfectly competitive firm:

- **AR = P** (average revenue is always price)
- **MR = P** (each extra unit sells at the same price)
- The firm's demand curve is **perfectly elastic** (horizontal) at the market price.

This horizontal line is labelled AR = MR = D = P on the firm diagram. It is vital to separate the two diagrams Edexcel expects you to link: the **industry** (market) diagram, with a normal downward-sloping demand curve and upward-sloping supply curve that sets the price; and the **firm** diagram, with the horizontal AR = MR line at that price and the firm's U-shaped cost curves.

The firm maximises profit where **MC = MR**, with MC rising (cutting MR from below). Since MR = P, this means the firm produces where **P = MC**. This has an important implication: the firm's MC curve above minimum average variable cost is its **short-run supply curve**, because for any price the firm will supply the output where MC equals that price. Adding the MC curves of all firms horizontally gives the industry supply curve.

Remember that MC must cut both AVC and AC at their minimum points. This is not a drawing convention but a mathematical necessity: when the marginal cost is below the average, it pulls the average down; when above, it pulls the average up; so the average is at its lowest exactly where they are equal.

sections.heading: Short-run equilibrium: supernormal profit, losses and shutdown
sections.body:
In the short run the number of firms is fixed, so the market price can be above or below average cost.

**Supernormal profit.** If the market price (P1) is above AC at the MC = MR output, the firm earns supernormal profit equal to (AR – AC) × Q, the shaded rectangle on the first diagram. This is profit above the minimum needed to keep the firm in the industry (normal profit, which is included in AC as the opportunity cost of the entrepreneur).

**Losses.** If demand falls and the price drops to P2, below AC at the profit-maximising output, the firm makes a loss of (AC – AR) × Q. It still produces where MC = MR because that **minimises** the loss.

**Short-run shutdown.** Should a loss-making firm close straight away? In the short run fixed costs must be paid whether or not it produces. So it should keep producing if price covers **average variable cost** (P ≥ AVC). Every unit then covers its variable cost and makes some contribution to fixed costs, so the loss is smaller than the fixed costs it would lose by shutting down. If P < AVC, each unit adds more to costs than to revenue, so it should stop producing immediately. The **shutdown point** is therefore the minimum of AVC, where MC cuts AVC.

**Long-run exit.** In the long run all costs are variable, so the firm leaves the industry unless P ≥ AC. The long-run shutdown point is the minimum of AC.

This gives a precise A* chain: a fall in market price that leaves P between minimum AVC and minimum AC means firms stay in the short run but begin to exit in the long run, shifting market supply left and pushing price back up.

sections.heading: From the short run to the long run
sections.body:
The defining feature of perfect competition is how free entry and exit eliminate supernormal profit and losses.

**Case 1: supernormal profit.** Suppose the market price P1 gives typical firms supernormal profit.
- Perfect information means outsiders know profits are high.
- No barriers to entry mean new firms join the market.
- Industry supply shifts right (S1 to S2 on the industry diagram).
- The market price falls, and each firm's horizontal AR = MR line shifts down.
- Entry continues until price equals **minimum AC**, where firms earn only normal profit and there is no incentive for more entry.

**Case 2: losses.** If the price is below AC, some firms leave in the long run. Industry supply shifts left, price rises and the remaining firms return to normal profit at minimum AC.

So in **long-run equilibrium**: P = AR = MR = MC = minimum AC. Each firm produces Q* at the lowest point of its AC curve and earns normal profit only.

Two further points earn credit:
- The long-run industry supply curve in a constant-cost industry is horizontal at minimum AC. If the industry's expansion pushes up input prices (an increasing-cost industry), long-run supply slopes upward.
- The adjustment takes time. In agriculture, a farmer can only change crops once a year, so markets can overshoot (the cobweb pattern), with prices swinging above and below the long-run level.

sections.heading: Efficiency in perfect competition
sections.body:
Long-run equilibrium satisfies both static efficiency conditions.

- **Allocative efficiency (P = MC)**: the price consumers pay, which reflects the value they place on the last unit, equals the cost of the resources used to make it. Output is exactly what society wants, consumer plus producer surplus is maximised and there is no deadweight loss.
- **Productive efficiency (output at minimum AC)**: firms produce at the lowest possible average cost, so no resources are wasted.
- **No X-inefficiency**: any firm with slack costs above minimum AC would make a loss at the market price and be forced out. Competition disciplines management.
- **Consumer sovereignty**: firms must produce what consumers want at the lowest price or be driven out.

However, **dynamic efficiency** is the model's weak point. With only normal profit in the long run, firms have no retained supernormal profit to fund research and development. And with perfect information, any innovation would be copied immediately by rivals, so the innovator could not earn a return on it. This is Schumpeter's argument that some market power, and the temporary supernormal profit it brings, may be needed for innovation.

There are further limits. Firms are small, so they may not exploit economies of scale: if the minimum efficient scale is large relative to the market, a perfectly competitive industry would have higher costs than a few large firms. Homogeneous products also mean no choice or variety for consumers. And the model ignores externalities: if production creates external costs, P = MC (private) is not socially efficient.

sections.heading: How useful is an unrealistic model?
sections.body:
Students sometimes dismiss perfect competition because no market fits all its assumptions. An A* answer explains why it is still valuable and where its predictions do hold.

- **As a benchmark**: by showing the efficient outcome, it lets economists measure the cost of market power. The deadweight loss of monopoly or the excess capacity in monopolistic competition are all defined against it.
- **Predictive power**: markets close to the assumptions behave as the model predicts. When wheat prices spiked after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, farmers worldwide planted more, and prices fell back over the following seasons as supply expanded.
- **Policy**: competition authorities such as the CMA aim to make markets behave more like competitive ones, by lowering barriers to entry, improving information (for example, requiring clear price comparison) and preventing collusion.

Weaknesses to evaluate:
- **Perfect information** is rare; consumers face search costs, and behavioural economics shows they do not always compare prices.
- **Homogeneous products** are rare; even commodity sellers try to differentiate (organic, local, Fairtrade).
- **Price taking** is broken whenever buyers are large. UK farmers sell into a highly concentrated supermarket sector, so they are price takers facing a monopsony buyer rather than a competitive market.
- **Entry is rarely free**: land, licences and capital can all be barriers.

The judgement: the model is a simplification whose usefulness depends on the question. It is excellent for explaining long-run price trends in commodity markets and for defining efficiency, but poor for predicting behaviour in markets dominated by brands, innovation or large firms.

key_terms.definition: A market structure with many small firms selling homogeneous products, perfect information and no barriers to entry or exit, so every firm is a price taker.
A firm that must accept the market price because it is too small to influence it and its product is identical to rivals'; it faces a perfectly elastic demand curve.
Output that consumers regard as identical whichever firm produces it, so the products are perfect substitutes.
The minimum profit needed to keep a firm in its current industry; it is the opportunity cost of the resources used and is included in average cost.
Profit above normal profit, where total revenue exceeds total cost (AR > AC); it signals entry when barriers are absent.
The price equal to minimum average variable cost; below it a firm minimises losses by ceasing production immediately.
The price equal to minimum average cost; below it a firm leaves the industry in the long run.
Producing the combination of goods consumers value most, where price equals marginal cost.
Producing at the lowest point of the average cost curve, so output is made with the fewest resources per unit.
Improvements in efficiency over time through investment, innovation and new products and processes.

diagrams.title: Perfectly competitive firm: short-run supernormal profit
diagrams.caption: The price taker produces Q1 where MC = MR. Because P1 exceeds AC1 at that output, the shaded rectangle (P1 – AC1) × Q1 is supernormal profit, which attracts new entrants.

diagrams.title: Short-run loss: keep producing while P ≥ AVC
diagrams.caption: At P2 the firm cannot cover average cost, so it makes the shaded loss. Price is still above average variable cost, so it covers all variable costs and contributes to fixed costs: it produces in the short run. Below minimum AVC (the shutdown point) it would close.

diagrams.title: Industry adjustment: entry shifts market supply right
diagrams.caption: Supernormal profit at P1 attracts entry. Market supply shifts from S1 to S2 until price falls to P2, the minimum of the typical firm's AC curve, where only normal profit is earned and entry stops.

diagrams.title: Long-run equilibrium of the perfectly competitive firm
diagrams.caption: In the long run price settles at the minimum of AC. The firm produces Q* where P = MC (allocatively efficient) and AC is at its lowest (productively efficient), earning normal profit only.

formulae.name: Supernormal profit
formulae.formula: (AR – AC) × Q
formulae.example: Market price £6, AC at the MC = MR output £3.50, output 750 units: profit = (6 – 3.50) × 750 = £1,875 supernormal profit.

formulae.name: Short-run production rule
formulae.formula: Produce if P ≥ AVC; shut down if P < AVC
formulae.example: P = £2.70, AVC = £2.50, AC = £3.27 at the chosen output: the firm makes a loss of £0.57 per unit but covers variable costs and contributes £0.20 per unit to fixed costs, so it keeps producing in the short run.

formulae.name: Long-run equilibrium condition
formulae.formula: P = AR = MR = MC = minimum AC
formulae.example: If minimum AC is £3.24, the long-run market price settles at £3.24 and each firm earns normal profit.

applications: UK and world wheat: thousands of farms sell a near-homogeneous product at a price set on international commodity markets. After the 2022 price spike following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, higher prices encouraged more planting, and prices fell back over 2023–24 as supply responded: the short-run to long-run adjustment of the model, slowed by the annual growing cycle.

Foreign exchange: sterling is traded by huge numbers of banks and institutions, the product (a pound) is identical and prices are visible instantly on screens, so no single trader can set the price. This is one of the closest real examples of price taking.

Online marketplaces for standard goods (for example identical phone chargers on Amazon or eBay) approach perfect information because price comparison is instant, and sellers who price above rivals sell almost nothing, although delivery times and reviews create some differentiation.

Globally, smallholder coffee and cocoa farmers are price takers. When world cocoa prices more than doubled during 2024 because of poor West African harvests, the high prices encouraged new planting elsewhere, but because cocoa trees take several years to mature, long-run supply adjustment is slow.
evaluation: Realism of assumptions: no market has perfect information and fully homogeneous products, so the long-run outcome of normal profit at minimum AC is a tendency rather than a description.
Time period: adjustment from short-run supernormal profit to long-run equilibrium can take years where production cycles are long (crops, mining), so short-run profits or losses may persist.

Dynamic efficiency: normal profit and instant imitation leave little incentive or finance for innovation, so a less competitive market may deliver lower costs and better products over time (Schumpeter).

Economies of scale: if minimum efficient scale is large relative to market demand, many small firms would have higher average costs than a few large ones, so perfect competition would be productively inefficient compared with oligopoly.

Externalities: allocative efficiency here is P = private MC; where production causes pollution (for example fertiliser run-off from farming), the competitive outcome overproduces relative to the social optimum.
Buyer power: many 'competitive' producers sell to concentrated buyers, so prices are shaped by monopsony power rather than competitive market forces.
Value as a benchmark: even if unrealistic, the model defines efficiency and so is essential for judging other market structures and competition policy.
misconceptions: Drawing the firm's demand curve downward sloping. The perfectly competitive firm's AR = MR line is horizontal; only the industry demand curve slopes down.
Thinking a loss-making firm must close at once. In the short run it keeps producing as long as price covers AVC, because fixed costs are paid anyway.
Saying firms earn zero profit in the long run. They earn normal profit, which is a cost included in AC; it is supernormal profit that is zero.
Drawing MC cutting AC anywhere other than its minimum point. MC must pass through the lowest point of both AVC and AC.
Assuming perfect competition is best in every respect. It achieves static efficiency but may lack dynamic efficiency and economies of scale.
exam_tips: Draw linked industry and firm diagrams side by side when explaining long-run adjustment: the market sets the price and the firm's AR = MR line moves with it.
Always label the profit or loss rectangle precisely: height AR – AC at the MC = MR output, width Q. Examiners check that the rectangle starts at the correct AC level.
For efficiency questions, state the condition (P = MC, minimum AC) and show it on the long-run diagram, then evaluate with dynamic efficiency and economies of scale.
In data responses, use the characteristics to judge how close a real market is to perfect competition, then explain which prediction this changes; do not just list the assumptions.
Use the shutdown condition for Paper 1 short-answer questions: P < AVC means immediate shutdown, AVC ≤ P < AC means produce in the short run but exit in the long run.

model_answer.question: Evaluate the view that perfectly competitive markets always produce the best outcome for consumers. (15 marks)
model_answer.answer:
Perfect competition is a market structure with many small firms selling homogeneous products, with perfect information and no barriers to entry or exit, so each firm is a price taker facing a horizontal AR = MR curve at the market price.

The main argument that this benefits consumers comes from the long-run equilibrium. Suppose firms are earning supernormal profit at price P1, because AR exceeds AC at the profit-maximising output where MC = MR. Perfect information means potential entrants know about these profits and the absence of barriers means they can enter. Industry supply shifts right from S1 to S2, the market price falls and each firm's AR = MR line shifts down. This continues until price equals minimum AC at P2, where firms earn only normal profit. In this equilibrium P = MC, so the firm is allocatively efficient: the value consumers place on the last unit equals its marginal cost, so there is no deadweight loss and consumer surplus is as large as possible. Firms also produce at minimum AC, so they are productively efficient, and any firm with slack costs would make losses and be forced out, so X-inefficiency is eliminated. For consumers this means the lowest sustainable price: compared with a monopoly setting price above MC, consumers pay less and buy more.

However, this ignores dynamic efficiency. In the long run firms earn only normal profit, so they have no retained supernormal profit to finance research and development. Even if a firm did innovate, perfect information means rivals would copy the improvement immediately, so it could not earn a return. Consumers may therefore pay lower prices today but miss out on better products and falling costs in future. Large firms in oligopolistic markets, such as pharmaceutical companies, use supernormal profit to fund innovation that perfectly competitive firms could not.

A second limitation is economies of scale. Each perfectly competitive firm is small. If the minimum efficient scale in an industry is large, as in car manufacturing or electricity networks, a market of many small firms would have a minimum AC well above that of a few large firms. A monopolist or oligopolist exploiting economies of scale could then charge a lower price than the perfectly competitive one, even after adding a profit margin.

Thirdly, homogeneous products mean consumers have no choice. Many consumers value variety and are willing to pay for differentiated products, so a market offering identical goods may not maximise their welfare even if prices are low.

Finally, the outcome is efficient only in private terms. If production generates negative externalities, P = private MC means output is above the socially optimal level.

Overall, perfect competition delivers the best outcome for consumers in terms of static efficiency: the lowest price for a given technology. But the word 'always' is too strong. Whether it is best depends on the industry: where economies of scale are small and innovation is limited, such as agricultural commodities, competition does deliver low prices and responsive supply. Where economies of scale are large and innovation drives consumer gains, such as pharmaceuticals or technology, some market power may produce lower long-run prices and better products. The most important factor is the size of the minimum efficient scale relative to the market, because that determines whether competition among many small firms is even possible without sacrificing lower costs.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: precise definition and accurate use of P = MC and minimum AC. Application: examples matched to the argument (agriculture versus pharmaceuticals and networks). Analysis: a full chain from supernormal profit through entry, supply shift and falling price to efficiency, referring to the linked diagrams. Evaluation: four distinct counter-arguments (dynamic efficiency, economies of scale, choice, externalities), each explained rather than listed, and a final judgement that addresses 'always' and identifies the deciding factor.

check.q: Why does a perfectly competitive firm face a perfectly elastic demand curve?
options: Its product is identical to rivals' and buyers have perfect information, so any price rise loses all sales
It has high fixed costs
Market demand is perfectly elastic
The government sets the price
check.explanation: Homogeneous products and perfect information mean the firm loses every customer if it charges above the market price, so its own demand curve is horizontal even though market demand slopes down.

check.q: A perfectly competitive firm's price is £4, its AVC is £3.50 and its AC is £4.60 at the MC = MR output. In the short run it should
options: shut down immediately because it is making a loss
continue producing because price covers AVC
raise its price to £4.60
increase output until AC equals £4
check.explanation: Price exceeds AVC, so each unit contributes 50p towards fixed costs. Closing would mean losing all fixed costs, which is worse. It would exit in the long run if price stays below AC.

check.q: Which describes long-run equilibrium in perfect competition?
options: P > MC and output below minimum AC
P = MC = minimum AC, with normal profit
MR = MC with supernormal profit protected by barriers
AR = AC on the falling part of the AC curve
check.explanation: Entry and exit remove supernormal profits and losses until price equals minimum AC, where P = MC as well.

check.q: The weakest aspect of efficiency under perfect competition is usually said to be
options: allocative efficiency
productive efficiency
dynamic efficiency
X-efficiency
check.explanation: Normal profit leaves little to fund R&D and perfect information allows instant copying, so incentives to innovate are weak.

check.q: What happens in a perfectly competitive industry when firms are making supernormal profit?
options: Firms exit, shifting supply left
New firms enter, shifting supply right and lowering price
Demand shifts right until profits disappear
Firms raise prices to maximise profit
check.explanation: With no barriers to entry, supernormal profit attracts entrants. Industry supply shifts right and price falls until only normal profit remains.

title: Monopolistic competition
overview: Monopolistic competition combines features of perfect competition (many firms, low barriers to entry) with a feature of monopoly (each firm sells a differentiated product and so faces a downward-sloping demand curve). It describes many everyday markets such as restaurants, hairdressers and independent retailers. You need to draw the short-run and long-run diagrams, including the tangency of AR and AC, and evaluate the efficiency of the outcome.
objectives: State the characteristics of monopolistic competition and give real examples
Explain why each firm faces a downward-sloping but relatively elastic demand curve
Draw short-run supernormal profit and the long-run tangency equilibrium
Explain excess capacity and why the long-run outcome is neither allocatively nor productively efficient
Evaluate whether the costs of inefficiency are outweighed by the benefits of choice and variety

sections.heading: Characteristics
sections.body:
The model was developed by Edward Chamberlin in the 1930s to describe markets that are neither perfectly competitive nor monopolised. Its characteristics are:

- **Many buyers and sellers**: each firm has a small market share, so firms act independently and do not need to consider rivals' reactions (unlike oligopoly).
- **Differentiated products**: each firm's product is slightly different, by location, quality, brand, style or service. A café on your street is not a perfect substitute for one two miles away.
- **Low barriers to entry and exit**: setting up a hair salon or a takeaway needs relatively little capital, and much of it (equipment) can be resold.
- **Firms are profit maximisers** (MC = MR) and have some, but limited, price-making power.

Because products are differentiated, a firm that raises its price does not lose all its customers, as some are loyal or value its location. So it faces a **downward-sloping demand curve**. But because there are many close substitutes, demand is **relatively price elastic**: a large price rise would lose many customers. On the diagram, draw AR fairly shallow, with MR below it and twice as steep.

Examples: restaurants and takeaways, hairdressers and barbers, plumbers and electricians, independent clothing shops, estate agents and many online sellers of craft goods. In each case there are many firms, each offering something slightly distinctive, and entry is easy.

sections.heading: Short-run equilibrium
sections.body:
In the short run the firm behaves like a small monopolist. It produces where **MC = MR** and sets the price from the AR curve at that output.

If demand for its product is strong, for example a new restaurant that becomes fashionable, AR lies above AC at the profit-maximising output and the firm makes **supernormal profit** equal to (AR – AC) × Q. This is shown as the shaded rectangle on the first diagram, with price P1, average cost AC1 and output Q1.

If demand is weak, AR may lie below AC at every output and the firm makes a loss. As with any firm, it continues producing in the short run as long as price covers average variable cost.

Why is the firm's short-run position important? Because, unlike in monopoly, the supernormal profit cannot last. The key difference from monopoly is low barriers to entry. Supernormal profit is a signal that attracts rivals offering similar, though not identical, products.

Note that firms in monopolistic competition will often use **non-price competition** to try to protect short-run profits: advertising, loyalty schemes, improving service quality or developing a stronger brand. The aim is to shift their demand curve right and make it less elastic, so that they can charge a higher price without losing as many customers. This adds costs, which shifts AC upward, a point worth using in evaluation.

sections.heading: Long-run equilibrium: the tangency solution
sections.body:
Because barriers to entry are low, supernormal profit attracts new firms. Each entrant takes some customers from existing firms, so each existing firm's demand (AR) curve **shifts left** and becomes **more elastic** as there are more close substitutes.

Entry continues until supernormal profit has been competed away. This happens when the AR curve is just **tangent to the AC curve** at the output where MC = MR. At that output AR = AC, so the firm makes **normal profit** only. If AR cut through AC, there would be a range of output where AR > AC and so profit to be made; tangency means the best the firm can do is break even.

If firms are making losses, the process works in reverse: some leave, the remaining firms' demand curves shift right until tangency is restored.

Geometrically, three things are true at the long-run output Q2:
- MR = MC (profit maximisation)
- AR = AC (normal profit, tangency)
- the tangency must be on the **downward-sloping part of AC**, because the AR curve slopes downward. AC is at its minimum further to the right, at Qmin.

This last point is the source of the model's key result: **excess capacity**. The firm produces less than the output that would minimise average cost. The gap between Q2 and Qmin is excess capacity; each firm could produce more at lower average cost, but it cannot sell more without cutting its price below average cost.

Compare this with perfect competition, where the horizontal AR line is tangent to AC at its minimum. The difference arises entirely from product differentiation.

sections.heading: Efficiency
sections.body:
Use the long-run diagram to assess each type of efficiency.

- **Allocative efficiency: not achieved.** At Q2, P2 is above MC, because the firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve and so MR < P. Consumers value an extra unit at more than its marginal cost, so output is lower than socially optimal. However, because demand is fairly elastic, the gap between P and MC is usually small, so the deadweight loss is much smaller than under monopoly.
- **Productive efficiency: not achieved.** Output is below Qmin, so average cost is above the minimum. Too many firms each produce too little: the high street may have five half-empty cafés where three busy ones could serve the same customers at lower average cost.
- **X-efficiency: largely achieved.** Firms only earn normal profit in the long run, so slack management that raises costs would mean losses and exit. Competition provides discipline.
- **Dynamic efficiency: limited.** Long-run normal profit leaves little to reinvest, and innovations (a new menu idea) are easy for rivals to copy. But in the short run firms do innovate to gain temporary supernormal profit, so there is some product innovation.

The major counterweight is **choice and variety**. Excess capacity can be seen as the price consumers pay for differentiated products. People value being able to choose between Thai, Italian and Turkish restaurants, or a barber close to home. If they were forced into a smaller number of identical firms, average costs might fall but welfare could be lower. This makes the evaluation genuinely two-sided.

sections.heading: Real-world complications
sections.body:
The model is a useful description of many local service markets, but several features of real markets complicate it.

- **Branding blurs the boundary with oligopoly.** In UK coffee shops, a small number of chains (Costa, Starbucks, Caffè Nero, plus Greggs and Pret in food-to-go) control a large share of branded outlets, while thousands of independents compete locally. The branded segment behaves more like an oligopoly, with interdependence; the independent fringe looks like monopolistic competition.
- **Persistent supernormal profit.** Strong brands, good locations and loyal customers can let some firms earn supernormal profit for years, because a location cannot easily be copied. Low barriers do not mean zero barriers.
- **Advertising costs.** Firms spend on marketing to differentiate, raising AC. Critics argue this is wasteful; supporters argue it gives information and funds variety.
- **Digital platforms.** Delivery apps such as Deliveroo and Just Eat have lowered entry barriers further (dark kitchens can open with little capital) but also made prices and reviews easier to compare, making demand more elastic and pushing firms closer to the competitive outcome.
- **High failure rates.** Entry and exit are frequent: many new restaurants close within a few years, which is consistent with the model's prediction that supernormal profit is quickly competed away.

These observations let you evaluate: the model's predictions hold most strongly where products are only slightly differentiated and entry is genuinely cheap.

key_terms.definition: A market structure with many firms selling differentiated products, low barriers to entry and exit, and independent decision-making.
Making a product distinct from rivals' through quality, branding, design, location or service, so it is not a perfect substitute.
Competing through means other than price, such as advertising, branding, quality, loyalty schemes and customer service.
The long-run equilibrium in which each firm's AR curve just touches its AC curve at the MC = MR output, so only normal profit is earned.
The difference between the firm's long-run output and the output at which average cost is minimised; the firm could produce more at lower unit cost.
The minimum profit needed to keep resources in their current use; earned when AR = AC.
A situation where price exceeds marginal cost, so too little of the good is produced relative to the social optimum.

diagrams.title: Monopolistic competition: short-run supernormal profit
diagrams.caption: Product differentiation gives each firm a downward-sloping (but quite price-elastic) demand curve. In the short run it produces where MC = MR and, if P1 > AC1, earns the shaded supernormal profit.

diagrams.title: Monopolistic competition: long-run equilibrium
diagrams.caption: Entry shifts each firm's demand left until AR is tangent to AC at the MC = MR output: only normal profit. Output Q2 is below Qmin (excess capacity), so the firm is not productively efficient, and P2 > MC, so it is not allocatively efficient.

applications: UK hairdressing and barbering: tens of thousands of small businesses, each differentiated by location, style and stylist, with low start-up costs (a chair can be rented in an existing salon). The boom in barber shops on many high streets in the late 2010s, followed by closures, illustrates entry competing away profits.

Restaurants and takeaways: low capital requirements and leased premises mean entry is easy, and delivery apps have reduced barriers further through 'dark kitchens'. Insolvency figures show hospitality has one of the highest business failure rates in the UK, consistent with profits being competed away and losses forcing exit.

Local trades such as plumbers and electricians: many sole traders, each differentiated by reputation, reviews and availability. Online review platforms improve information, making demand more price elastic.
Globally, street food and small retailers in cities from Bangkok to Lagos fit the model closely: many sellers, slight differences in recipes and location, and almost no barriers to entry.
evaluation: Choice versus efficiency: excess capacity and P > MC are costs, but they buy variety that consumers value; welfare may be higher than in a market of fewer, identical, lower-cost firms.
Magnitude of inefficiency: because demand is relatively elastic, the gap between price and MC and between Q2 and Qmin is small, so the welfare loss is much less than under monopoly.
Barriers are low but not zero: good locations, reputation and brand loyalty can allow supernormal profit to persist, so the long-run tangency outcome may not be reached.
Non-price competition raises costs: advertising and branding shift AC upwards; whether this is waste or useful information depends on the product.
Boundary with oligopoly: where a few chains dominate (coffee shops, gyms), firms are interdependent and the model predicts less well than oligopoly theory.
Dynamic efficiency: short-run supernormal profit gives some incentive to innovate, but easy imitation limits the returns, so innovation is mainly small product tweaks rather than major R&D.
misconceptions: Drawing the long-run tangency at the minimum of AC. Because AR slopes down, the tangency is on the falling part of AC, to the left of the minimum.
Drawing MR = MC at a different output from the tangency. In long-run equilibrium MR = MC and AR = AC must occur at the same output.
Saying firms in monopolistic competition are interdependent. With many small firms, each acts independently; interdependence is the defining feature of oligopoly.
Assuming differentiated products mean high barriers to entry. Differentiation gives some price-setting power, but entry remains easy.
exam_tips: Get the long-run diagram right: AR tangent to AC, MR = MC vertically below the tangency, Qmin marked to the right to show excess capacity.
When asked about efficiency, compare explicitly with perfect competition (P = MC = min AC) and monopoly (large deadweight loss), so you show the structure sits between them.
In data questions, identify the characteristics in the extract (number of firms, ease of entry, differentiation) before applying the model.
Evaluation marks come from weighing the inefficiency against choice and variety, and from questioning whether barriers are really low.

model_answer.question: Assess whether firms in monopolistically competitive markets, such as restaurants, are economically efficient in the long run. (12 marks)
model_answer.answer:
Monopolistic competition is a market structure with many firms selling differentiated products and low barriers to entry and exit. Restaurants fit well: there are thousands in the UK, each differentiated by cuisine, location and atmosphere, and premises can be leased with relatively little capital.

Because each restaurant's meals are differentiated, it faces a downward-sloping but fairly price-elastic demand curve. In the short run a popular restaurant produces where MC = MR and may earn supernormal profit if AR > AC. However, low barriers to entry mean this attracts new restaurants offering similar meals. Each existing restaurant loses customers, so its AR curve shifts left and becomes more elastic until it is tangent to AC at the MC = MR output, Q2. At this point AR = AC, so only normal profit is earned.

This long-run equilibrium is productively inefficient. The AR curve slopes downward, so the tangency with AC must lie on the falling part of AC, to the left of the minimum at Qmin. Each restaurant therefore operates with excess capacity, for example tables that are empty on most weeknights, and average cost is higher than it could be. It is also allocatively inefficient, because at Q2 the price P2 is above MC: diners value an extra meal at more than it costs to produce, so output is below the socially optimal level and there is a deadweight loss.

However, the scale of these inefficiencies is limited. Because there are many close substitutes, demand is fairly elastic, so the gap between price and MC is small and the tangency is close to minimum AC. The welfare loss is much smaller than in a monopoly. Restaurants are also likely to be X-efficient, since with only normal profit, any restaurant with slack costs would make losses and close, as the high failure rate in hospitality suggests.

More importantly, the static efficiency criteria ignore the value of variety. Excess capacity is partly the cost of having many different restaurants. If the market had fewer, larger restaurants all serving the same food, average costs might fall, but consumers would lose choice they clearly value, since they are willing to pay slightly more for differentiation. Static efficiency measures do not capture this benefit.

Overall, restaurants in monopolistic competition are not efficient by the strict definitions of allocative and productive efficiency, but the inefficiency is small and is largely the price of choice. The judgement depends on how differentiated the products are: the more consumers value the difference between restaurants, the stronger the case that the outcome is efficient in a broader welfare sense.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge and application: accurate characteristics applied throughout to restaurants. Analysis: a complete chain from short-run profit through entry to tangency, linked to the diagram, with clear explanations of why tangency lies left of minimum AC and why P > MC. Evaluation: magnitude of inefficiency, X-efficiency and the value of variety, ending in a judgement that identifies what it depends on.

Its product is differentiated from rivals' products
Barriers to entry are high
It colludes with rivals

options: P = MC = minimum AC
AR = AC on the falling part of the AC curve
AR > AC because of barriers to entry

firms produce less than the output that minimises average cost
firms earn supernormal profit in the long run
firms produce where P = MC

It is productively efficient but not allocatively efficient
It is neither allocatively nor productively efficient
It is allocatively efficient but not productively efficient

title: Oligopoly
overview: Oligopoly is a market dominated by a few large, interdependent firms, and it describes many of the UK's most important markets: supermarkets, banking, energy supply, mobile networks and airlines. Because each firm's best decision depends on what rivals do, there is no single oligopoly model: you need concentration ratios, collusion and cartels, game theory, the kinked demand curve and the types of price and non-price competition. It is examined heavily in Paper 1 and Paper 3 data responses and essays.
objectives: Define oligopoly and explain its characteristics, especially interdependence and barriers to entry
Calculate and interpret n-firm concentration ratios
Explain overt and tacit collusion, cartels, and the conditions that make collusion likely to succeed or break down
Use a two-firm payoff matrix to explain the prisoners' dilemma, dominant strategies and Nash equilibrium
Draw and explain the kinked demand curve and evaluate its limitations
Analyse price competition (price wars, predatory and limit pricing) and non-price competition, and evaluate the outcomes for consumers

sections.heading: Characteristics and concentration ratios
sections.body:
An oligopoly is a market dominated by a few large firms. Its characteristics are:

- **High barriers to entry and exit**: economies of scale, brand loyalty, control of supply chains, patents, high sunk costs (advertising, networks) and sometimes licences.
- **Interdependence**: each firm's decisions on price, output and advertising affect its rivals, so every firm must anticipate how rivals will react. This is the defining feature that separates oligopoly from all other structures.
- **Products may be differentiated** (cars, smartphones, supermarkets) or **homogeneous** (cement, steel, oil).
- **Firms may compete or collude**, so outcomes range from near-competitive to near-monopoly.

**Concentration ratios** measure market structure. An **n-firm concentration ratio** is the combined market share of the n largest firms. A common rule of thumb is that a market is an oligopoly if the **five-firm ratio exceeds about 60%** (some textbooks use the four-firm ratio above about 50%).

Worked example: shares are 28%, 19%, 13%, 11%, 9%, 8%, 6% and 6%. The three-firm ratio is 28 + 19 + 13 = 60%. The five-firm ratio is 28 + 19 + 13 + 11 + 9 = 80%: clearly oligopolistic.

In the UK grocery market around 2025, Tesco had roughly 27–28%, Sainsbury's around 15%, Asda around 12%, Aldi around 10% and Morrisons and Lidl around 8% each, giving a four-firm ratio of roughly 65%.

Evaluate the measure: a concentration ratio ignores the **distribution** of shares within the top firms (80% split 76/1/1/1/1 is very different from 16% each), says nothing about **conduct** (are firms colluding?), depends on how the market is **defined** (national or local, all groceries or online only), and ignores **contestability** and import competition. The Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (sum of squared market shares) is a better measure of inequality between firms and is used by competition authorities.

sections.heading: Collusion and cartels
Game theory: the prisoners' dilemma
sections.body:
Game theory models interdependent decisions. A simple two-firm, two-strategy game shows why oligopolists often end up competing even though collusion would pay more.

Two supermarkets, A and B, each choose a **high price** or a **low price**. The payoff matrix gives annual profits (A's profit first, B's second):

- Both charge high: A £10m, B £10m.
- A low, B high: A £14m, B £4m (A wins customers from B).
- A high, B low: A £4m, B £14m.
- Both charge low: A £6m, B £6m.

**Find A's best response to each B choice.** If B charges high, A earns 14 by going low versus 10 by staying high: choose low. If B charges low, A earns 6 by going low versus 4 by going high: choose low. So low price is A's **dominant strategy**, the best choice whatever the rival does. By symmetry it is B's dominant strategy too.

The result is that both charge low and earn £6m each. This is a **Nash equilibrium**: neither firm can gain by changing its strategy, given the other's choice. Yet both would be better off at (high, high) earning £10m. This is the **prisoners' dilemma**: individually rational decisions lead to a collectively worse outcome.

What changes the outcome?
- **Repeated games**: if the game is played every week, firms can use strategies such as **tit-for-tat** (match whatever the rival did last time). The threat of retaliation makes cheating less attractive, so tacit collusion at high prices can be sustained.
- **Communication and binding agreements** (illegal cartels) remove uncertainty.
- **First-mover advantages** in sequential games, such as committing to build large capacity to deter entry.
- **Leniency** creates a new prisoners' dilemma for cartel members: each fears the other will confess first.

For consumers, the competitive Nash equilibrium is good news: lower prices. Game theory explains why price wars happen and why collusion is unstable.

sections.heading: The kinked demand curve
sections.body:
The kinked demand curve model explains **price rigidity**: why prices in oligopoly often stay stable even when costs change.

Assume the current price is P* and each firm believes:
- if it **raises** its price, rivals will **not** follow, hoping to win its customers. Demand above P* is therefore **price elastic**: a price rise loses a large share of sales, so total revenue falls.
- if it **cuts** its price, rivals **will** follow to protect their market share. Demand below P* is therefore **price inelastic**: the price cut gains few customers, so total revenue falls.

So the demand (AR) curve is kinked at P*. Because MR is derived from AR, the elastic upper section has a shallow MR and the inelastic lower section has a steep MR, which starts much lower. The result is a **vertical discontinuity (gap) in MR** at Q*.

If MC passes anywhere through this gap, the profit-maximising output stays Q* and price stays P*. A rise in costs from MC1 to MC2 changes nothing, provided MC stays within the gap. This explains why firms may absorb cost changes and prefer to compete through non-price methods.

**Limitations** (strong evaluation material):
- It explains why the price stays at P* but not **how P* was set** in the first place.
- The assumption that rivals ignore price rises is often wrong. When costs rise across the industry, such as energy and food costs in 2022, all firms raise prices together, often following a price leader.
- Empirical evidence is mixed: prices in many oligopolies change frequently (airline and supermarket promotions).
- It assumes firms are profit maximisers and that the gap is large enough to contain cost changes.

sections.heading: Price competition
sections.body:
When oligopolists do compete on price, several strategies are used.

- **Price wars**: firms repeatedly undercut each other. Consumers gain in the short run, but weaker firms may exit, increasing concentration later. UK supermarkets fought intense price campaigns as Aldi and Lidl grew from the 2010s, with the big four matching discounter prices on key lines through schemes such as Aldi Price Match and loyalty card pricing.
- **Predatory pricing**: a dominant firm deliberately sets price **below average variable cost** to drive a rival out, planning to raise prices once the rival has gone. It is illegal as an abuse of dominance (Competition Act 1998, Chapter II), but hard to prove because it looks like vigorous competition. The firm must be able to survive losses longer than the rival, and must expect barriers to prevent re-entry afterwards.
- **Limit pricing**: incumbents set price at the highest level that **deters entry**, below the profit-maximising price, so that a new entrant with higher costs (no economies of scale yet) could not make a profit. This is legal and benefits consumers compared with monopoly pricing, but sacrifices some profit.
- **Price leadership**: one firm sets the price and others follow, a form of tacit collusion.

The outcome for consumers depends on the strategy. Short-term price competition lowers prices; predatory pricing harms consumers in the long run; limit pricing gives prices below the monopoly level. Evaluating which is happening requires evidence on costs, which is why competition authorities find these cases difficult.

sections.heading: Non-price competition and outcomes
sections.body:
Because price competition is risky (price wars cut everyone's profit) and price rises are not followed, oligopolists rely heavily on **non-price competition**:

- **Advertising and branding** to increase demand and make it more price inelastic, raising barriers to entry.
- **Product innovation and quality**: new models, features and own-label ranges.
- **Loyalty schemes**: Tesco Clubcard and Nectar prices give discounts only to members, collecting data and raising switching costs.
- **Customer service, delivery and opening hours**.
- **Bundling** (broadband, TV and mobile packages) and long contracts.

Non-price competition can **benefit consumers** through better products, wider choice and dynamic efficiency funded by supernormal profit (car and smartphone innovation). But it can also **raise costs**, shifting AC up and keeping prices high, and heavy advertising can act as a barrier to entry.

**Overall efficiency of oligopoly** depends on behaviour:
- If firms **collude**, the outcome resembles monopoly: P > MC, allocative inefficiency, deadweight loss and possibly X-inefficiency.
- If they **compete hard**, prices may approach costs, and large firms can exploit **economies of scale**, giving lower AC than a fragmented market could achieve.
- Supernormal profit can fund **R&D**, supporting dynamic efficiency.

This is why the UK's approach, through the CMA, is not to break up all oligopolies but to target collusion, abuse of dominance and mergers that would substantially lessen competition.

key_terms.definition: A market dominated by a few large, interdependent firms, protected by high barriers to entry.
The situation where each firm's decisions affect its rivals, so it must take their likely reactions into account.
The combined market share of the n largest firms in a market.
Cooperation between rival firms to limit competition, for example by fixing prices or sharing markets; it may be overt or tacit.
A formal agreement between firms to fix prices, restrict output or divide markets so that they act like a joint monopoly.
Coordination without an explicit agreement, for example by following a price leader.
A situation where one firm sets prices and rivals follow its changes.
A strategy that gives a player the best payoff whatever the other player does.
An outcome where no player can improve their payoff by changing strategy, given the strategies chosen by the others.
A game in which each player's dominant strategy leads to an outcome that is worse for both than if they had cooperated.
A model in which rivals match price cuts but not price rises, producing a kink in demand at the current price and a gap in MR that explains price rigidity.
Setting price below average variable cost to force a rival out of the market, with the intention of raising prices later.
Setting price below the profit-maximising level, at the highest level that still deters new firms from entering.

diagrams.title: Kinked demand curve
diagrams.caption: Rivals match price cuts but ignore price rises, so demand is elastic above P* and inelastic below it. MR is discontinuous at Q*; any MC curve passing through the vertical gap (MC1 to MC2) gives the same profit-maximising price P* and output Q*, which explains price rigidity.

diagrams.title: Collusion: the cartel acts like a monopolist
diagrams.caption: Colluding firms jointly restrict output to Qcartel, where industry MC = MR, and share out quotas. Price rises to Pcartel above the competitive level Pc. Each member could raise its own profit by secretly producing more at Pcartel, which is why cartels are unstable.

formulae.name: n-firm concentration ratio
formulae.formula: Sum of the market shares of the n largest firms

formulae.name: Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (extension)
formulae.formula: Sum of the squared market shares of all firms
formulae.example: Four firms with 40%, 30%, 20% and 10%: HHI = 1,600 + 900 + 400 + 100 = 3,000, a highly concentrated market.

formulae.name: Market share from sales
formulae.formula: Firm's sales ÷ total market sales × 100
formulae.example: Firm sales £4.2bn in a £30bn market: share = 14%.

applications: UK groceries: a four-firm concentration ratio of roughly 65% around 2025, intense non-price competition through Clubcard and Nectar loyalty pricing, and price matching against Aldi and Lidl. The CMA's 2023 review of grocery prices found no evidence that weak competition was the main cause of food inflation, showing that a high concentration ratio does not necessarily mean collusion.

Collusion and leniency: in 2007 British Airways was fined over £120m for colluding with Virgin Atlantic on long-haul fuel surcharges; Virgin escaped a fine by reporting the cartel first. In 2016 the European Commission fined truck manufacturers almost €3bn for a 14-year price cartel, one of the largest cartel fines ever.

UK mobile networks: the 2024 approval of the Vodafone–Three merger (with investment commitments and price protections) cut the number of network operators from four to three, increasing concentration. The CMA accepted it because the merged firm committed to around £11bn of network investment, an example of weighing static against dynamic efficiency.

OPEC+: oil producers agree output quotas to support prices, but compliance is uneven; members with high spending needs have repeatedly exceeded quotas, illustrating the incentive to cheat in a cartel.

Banking: the UK's large banks have long been concentrated in personal current accounts. Low switching rates, despite the Current Account Switch Service, show how inertia can sustain market power without collusion.
evaluation: Concentration ratio limits: it ignores the distribution of shares, firm conduct, market definition and contestability; a highly concentrated market can still be competitive if firms fight for market share.

Collusion versus competition: outcomes depend on behaviour, not just structure. Colluding oligopolists approach the monopoly outcome; competing ones may approach competitive prices while gaining economies of scale.
Stability of collusion depends on the number of firms, product similarity, cost similarity, market transparency, entry barriers and the effectiveness of competition law and leniency.

Game theory insights depend on assumptions: one-shot games predict competition, but repeated games make tacit collusion sustainable, so long-standing oligopolies may be less competitive than the simple matrix suggests.
Kinked demand curve: explains price stability but not how prices are set, and is contradicted when industry-wide cost shocks lead all firms to raise prices together.

Dynamic efficiency: supernormal profit can fund innovation (smartphones, pharmaceuticals), so oligopoly may beat perfect competition over time, though only if competition gives firms a reason to innovate.
Non-price competition can improve quality and choice or simply raise costs and barriers to entry; the effect is product specific.
misconceptions: Assuming oligopoly always means collusion and high prices. Many oligopolies compete fiercely; structure alone does not determine conduct.
Confusing a Nash equilibrium with the best joint outcome. In the prisoners' dilemma the Nash equilibrium is worse for both players than cooperation.
Drawing the kinked demand curve with MR continuous. MR must have a vertical gap at the kink output, and MC must pass through the gap.
Treating limit pricing and predatory pricing as the same. Limit pricing keeps price above cost to deter entry; predatory pricing sets price below AVC to eliminate a rival and is illegal.
Thinking tacit collusion is illegal in itself. Firms independently following a price leader is not unlawful; explicit agreements are.
exam_tips: Concentration ratio questions are quick marks: add the n largest shares, state whether the market is an oligopoly, and comment on one limitation.

For game theory, work through each player's best response explicitly, identify the dominant strategy and Nash equilibrium, then explain why the outcome is a dilemma. Then evaluate with repeated games.
Always draw the MR gap on the kinked demand diagram and show two MC curves passing through it.
For essay questions on whether oligopoly benefits consumers, organise the answer around 'it depends on whether firms collude or compete', using real UK examples and competition policy.
Use the cartel diagram (industry MC = MR) to show the effect of collusion on price, output and deadweight loss.

model_answer.question: Evaluate the likely impact on consumers of collusion between firms in an oligopolistic market. (15 marks)
model_answer.answer:
An oligopoly is a market dominated by a few large interdependent firms, usually with a five-firm concentration ratio above about 60%. Collusion occurs when these firms cooperate rather than compete, either overtly through a cartel that fixes prices or quotas, or tacitly, for example by following a price leader.

The main impact on consumers is higher prices and lower output. By colluding, firms can act as a joint monopolist. As shown on the cartel diagram, they restrict industry output to Qcartel, where industry MC = MR, and charge Pcartel from the demand curve, well above the competitive price Pc where P = MC. Consumers pay more, buy less, and part of consumer surplus is transferred to firms as supernormal profit. The triangle between Qcartel and Qc is a deadweight loss: units that consumers value above their marginal cost are not produced, so the outcome is allocatively inefficient. For example, the fuel surcharge collusion between British Airways and Virgin Atlantic raised the price of long-haul flights for passengers.

Collusion can also reduce choice and quality. Firms that are not competing on price have less pressure to control costs, so X-inefficiency may rise, pushing AC up. They may also divide up markets so consumers in each area effectively face a single supplier.

However, the scale of the harm depends on whether the collusion is stable. Game theory shows that each firm has an incentive to cheat. In a payoff matrix where both firms earn £10m by charging high prices, a firm that undercuts while its rival stays high might earn £14m, so cutting price is a dominant strategy and the Nash equilibrium is for both to charge low. In practice cartels break down when there are many firms, when products and costs differ, or when demand falls, so the period of high prices may be short. OPEC members exceeding their oil quotas shows how hard it is to maintain discipline.

The impact also depends on competition policy. In the UK, cartels are illegal under the Competition Act 1998, fines can reach 10% of worldwide turnover and leniency gives immunity to the first firm to confess. This creates a second prisoners' dilemma among cartel members, making overt collusion riskier. Tacit collusion is harder to detect, though, so consumers may still face prices above competitive levels in markets with stable price leaders.

Finally, some forms of cooperation can benefit consumers. Joint ventures in research, such as shared development of new technology, can raise dynamic efficiency, and stable supernormal profits can fund investment. However, these are different from price-fixing, which almost always harms consumers.

Overall, collusion that succeeds is clearly harmful to consumers, through higher prices, lower output and deadweight loss. The key question is how durable it is. The impact is greatest in markets with few firms, homogeneous products, high barriers to entry and transparent prices, because these make collusion stable and cheating easy to punish. Strong enforcement and leniency programmes reduce the harm by making cartels less stable.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: precise definitions of oligopoly, overt and tacit collusion. Application: BA and Virgin, OPEC, UK law. Analysis: the cartel diagram chain (industry MC = MR, higher price, deadweight loss) and a worked game theory argument with dominant strategy and Nash equilibrium. Evaluation: stability of collusion, the role of policy, the distinction between price-fixing and beneficial cooperation, ending in a judgement that names the conditions making harm greatest.

In the payoff matrix, both firms earn £10m if they charge high prices and £6m if both charge low. If one charges low and the other high, the low-price firm earns £14m and the other £4m. What is the Nash equilibrium?

Both charge low prices

ignore both price rises and price cuts
match price cuts but ignore price rises
match price rises but ignore price cuts
check.explanation: This makes demand elastic above the current price and inelastic below it, creating the kink and the gap in MR.

options: Only a small number of firms
Homogeneous products
Large differences in costs between members
High barriers to entry

setting price below average variable cost to drive out a rival
following the price set by a dominant firm
charging different prices to different consumers
