title: Monopoly
overview: A monopoly is a single seller (in theory) or a dominant firm (in practice) protected by barriers to entry. You must be able to draw profit maximisation with supernormal profit, show the welfare loss compared with competition, explain third-degree price discrimination and natural monopoly, and evaluate the costs and benefits of monopoly for consumers, firms, employees and suppliers. This is one of the most frequently examined topics in Theme 3 essays.
objectives: Distinguish pure monopoly from monopoly power and explain the sources of monopoly power
Draw and explain monopoly profit maximisation, including the supernormal profit rectangle, and the deadweight loss compared with competition
Explain the conditions for price discrimination and draw the third-degree price discrimination diagram
Draw and explain natural monopoly and the problem of pricing at P = MC
Evaluate the costs and benefits of monopoly for different stakeholders

sections.heading: Monopoly and monopoly power
sections.body:
A **pure monopoly** is a single firm supplying the whole market, with no close substitutes. In practice, UK competition law treats a firm with **25% or more of a market** as having monopoly power for merger purposes, and competition authorities look for **dominance**, typically market shares above 40%.

The characteristics of the model are:
- one dominant seller; the firm is the industry, so its demand curve is the market demand curve and slopes downward;
- the firm is a **price maker**, but it cannot choose both price and quantity: if it sets price, demand determines quantity;
- **high barriers to entry**, which allow supernormal profit to persist in the long run;
- the firm is assumed to be a profit maximiser.

The degree of monopoly power depends on:
- **Barriers to entry**: economies of scale, legal barriers (patents, licences, franchises), control of essential inputs or distribution, brand loyalty and advertising, network effects, sunk costs and anti-competitive tactics such as limit or predatory pricing.
- **The number and closeness of substitutes**: the fewer the substitutes, the less price-elastic demand is and the more power the firm has.
- **Advertising and product differentiation**, which reduce the elasticity of demand.

Examples include Network Rail (rail track), regional water companies such as Thames Water, Google in general search (around 90% of UK searches, designated by the CMA in 2025 as having strategic market status under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024), and pharmaceutical firms with patents on specific drugs.

sections.heading: Profit maximisation and supernormal profit
sections.body:
Because the monopolist faces the downward-sloping market demand curve, to sell an extra unit it must lower the price on all units. So **MR is below AR**. For a straight-line AR, MR has the same vertical intercept and is **twice as steep**, hitting the quantity axis halfway along. MR is zero at the midpoint of AR, where PED = 1, and negative beyond it.

The monopolist:
1. chooses output **Qm** where **MC = MR** (MC cutting MR from below);
2. charges the highest price consumers will pay for Qm, read up to the **AR curve**: **Pm**;
3. earns **supernormal profit** = (AR – AC) × Q = (Pm – ACm) × Qm, the shaded rectangle.

Because barriers to entry block new firms, the supernormal profit **persists in the long run**: this is the key difference from perfect and monopolistic competition.

Two results follow:
- A profit-maximising monopolist always produces on the **price-elastic** part of the demand curve, because MC is positive and MR must equal it, so MR > 0, which only happens where PED > 1.
- There is **no supply curve** for a monopolist: the quantity supplied at any price depends on the position and elasticity of demand, not just on MC.

**Welfare loss.** The second diagram compares monopoly with a competitive industry with the same constant costs. Competition would produce Qc at Pc = MC. The monopolist restricts output to Qm and raises price to Pm. The rectangle between Pm and Pc up to Qm is a transfer from consumer surplus to monopoly profit. The triangle between Qm and Qc is **deadweight loss**: units consumers value above their marginal cost that are not produced. The monopoly is **allocatively inefficient** (P > MC) and, since there is no reason for it to produce at minimum AC, generally **productively inefficient** too. Without competitive pressure it may also be **X-inefficient**.

sections.heading: Price discrimination
sections.body:
Price discrimination is charging **different prices to different consumers for the same good or service, for reasons not associated with differences in cost**. (Higher prices that reflect higher costs, such as delivery to remote areas, are not discrimination.)

**Conditions** required:
- the firm must have **price-making (monopoly) power**;
- it must be able to **separate the market** into groups (by time, age, location, income, status) and prevent **resale (arbitrage)** between them;
- the groups must have **different price elasticities of demand**.

**Types:**
- **First degree (perfect)**: each consumer is charged the maximum they are willing to pay, so all consumer surplus becomes producer surplus. Close examples are auctions and personalised online pricing.
- **Second degree**: different prices for different quantities or versions, such as bulk discounts or cheaper off-peak electricity.
- **Third degree**: different prices to different identifiable groups, such as peak and off-peak rail fares, student and pensioner discounts, or children's cinema tickets.

**The third-degree diagram.** With constant MC, the firm sets **MR = MC in each market**. In market A (inelastic demand, e.g. commuters who must travel at peak times), the MR = MC output QA is sold at the high price PA. In market B (elastic demand, e.g. leisure travellers), QB is sold at the lower price PB. The rule is that the **less elastic** group pays the **higher** price. Profit is higher than charging a single price, because the firm extracts more consumer surplus from inelastic buyers while still selling to price-sensitive ones.

**Evaluation.**
- **Costs to consumers**: consumer surplus is converted into producer surplus; those with inelastic demand pay more, which may be inequitable (people who cannot avoid peak travel).
- **Benefits**: some consumers pay less than under a single price and some who would have been priced out are now served (students, pensioners, off-peak leisure travellers), so output may rise. Extra profit may fund investment or cross-subsidise loss-making services, such as rural rail routes.
- **Efficiency**: perfect price discrimination produces where P = MC for the last unit, so output is allocatively efficient, though all surplus goes to the firm.

sections.heading: Natural monopoly
sections.body:
A **natural monopoly** exists when **one firm can supply the entire market at a lower average cost than two or more firms could**. This happens where fixed costs are enormous and marginal costs low, so **LRAC falls over the whole range of market demand**: economies of scale are never exhausted.

Examples are the infrastructure networks: the electricity and gas grids (National Grid), water and sewerage pipes, rail track (Network Rail) and the local telephone and broadband network (Openreach). Building a second set of water pipes to every house would double the fixed costs while splitting the customers, so average cost would be much higher.

On the diagram LRAC falls throughout and LRMC lies below it (when average cost is falling, marginal cost must be below the average). Three outcomes can be compared:
- **Unregulated profit maximisation**: Q1 where MC = MR, price P1, supernormal profit.
- **Allocatively efficient pricing (P = MC)**: Q3. Because LRAC is above LRMC at every output, P = MC means **price is below average cost and the firm makes a loss**. It would need a subsidy, or it would leave the market.
- **Average-cost pricing (P = AC)**: Q2 and P2, where AR cuts LRAC. The firm covers its costs including normal profit. Output is higher and price lower than under profit maximisation, but P > MC, so there is a small deadweight loss.

This is why natural monopolies are normally either **state-owned** or **privately owned but regulated** by bodies such as Ofwat, Ofgem and Ofcom, using price caps and performance targets. Competition is often introduced where possible in the parts of the industry that are not natural monopolies (energy supply, broadband retail), while the network remains a single regulated firm.

sections.heading: Costs and benefits of monopoly
sections.body:
The spec asks you to judge monopoly from the point of view of different stakeholders.

**Costs**
- **Consumers**: higher prices, lower output and less choice than under competition; loss of consumer surplus and deadweight loss (allocative inefficiency). Possible poor quality and service because customers have nowhere else to go.
- **Efficiency**: productive inefficiency and X-inefficiency, because supernormal profit is protected and managers face little pressure.
- **Suppliers**: a monopolist that is also a dominant buyer may use monopsony power to push down supplier prices.
- **Employees**: in a monopsony-style local labour market, lower wages; fewer jobs because output is restricted.
- **Equity**: profits flow to shareholders, often higher-income households, while price rises hit all consumers.

**Benefits**
- **Economies of scale**: large firms may have lower AC than many small firms, so even with a profit margin, prices could be lower than under competition. This is decisive for natural monopolies.
- **Dynamic efficiency**: supernormal profit can fund R&D. Patents deliberately grant temporary monopoly to reward innovation, as in pharmaceuticals where developing a new drug can cost over a billion pounds.
- **Cross-subsidisation and price discrimination** can extend supply to groups who would otherwise not be served.
- **Stability for employees**: profitable firms may offer secure jobs and pay above the market rate.
- **Global competitiveness**: a firm dominant in the UK may still face intense competition internationally, and needs scale to compete.

The key evaluation points: is the monopoly **contestable** (threat of entry keeps prices down)? Is it **regulated**? Does it earn its position through innovation (and will it continue to innovate), or by blocking entry? A judgement should weigh static losses against dynamic gains, considering the specific market.

key_terms.definition: A market structure in which a single firm supplies the entire market and there are no close substitutes.
The ability of a firm to set price above marginal cost without losing all its customers; in UK law a market share of 25% or more is a reference point for merger investigations.
Obstacles that make it difficult or impossible for new firms to enter a market, allowing incumbents to earn supernormal profit in the long run.
A firm with enough market power to set the price of its product, constrained by the demand curve.
The loss of consumer and producer surplus when output is below the allocatively efficient level, shown as a triangle between demand and MC.
Charging different prices to different consumers for the same product, for reasons not related to differences in cost.
Charging different prices to distinct groups of consumers with different price elasticities of demand, with the higher price charged to the less elastic group.
Buying in a low-price market and reselling in a high-price market; price discrimination requires it to be prevented.
A market in which one firm can supply total demand at a lower average cost than two or more firms, because LRAC falls over the whole range of output.
Using profits from one product or market to fund losses on another.
Producing at a cost above the lowest attainable for a given output, because of organisational slack when competitive pressure is weak.

diagrams.title: Monopoly profit maximisation
diagrams.caption: The monopolist chooses Qm where MC = MR, then charges the highest price consumers will pay for that output, read off the AR curve (Pm). Because Pm > ACm, the shaded area is supernormal profit, protected in the long run by barriers to entry. MR is twice as steep as AR.

diagrams.title: Monopoly versus competition: welfare loss
diagrams.caption: With constant costs a competitive industry would produce Qc at Pc = MC. A profit-maximising monopolist restricts output to Qm and raises price to Pm. Part of consumer surplus becomes profit; the triangle is deadweight welfare loss because P > MC between Qm and Qc.

diagrams.title: Third-degree price discrimination (constant MC)
diagrams.caption: The firm sets MR = MC separately in each market. Market A (e.g. peak-time business travellers) has less price-elastic demand, so its MR = MC output is sold at the high price PA; market B (elastic, e.g. off-peak leisure) pays the lower price PB.

diagrams.title: Natural monopoly
diagrams.caption: LRAC falls over the whole range of market demand because fixed costs are huge, so one firm can supply the market more cheaply than two. Unregulated, it produces Q1 at P1. Pricing at P = MC (Q3) is allocatively efficient but below LRAC, so the firm makes a loss; average-cost pricing (Q2, P2) gives normal profit.

formulae.name: Supernormal profit
formulae.formula: (AR – AC) × Q

formulae.name: Linear AR and MR
formulae.formula: If AR = a – bQ, then MR = a – 2bQ

formulae.name: Deadweight loss (linear)
formulae.formula: ½ × (Pm – MC) × (Qc – Qm)
formulae.example: Pm = £6, MC = £3, Qm = 3.75, Qc = 7.5: DWL = ½ × 3 × 3.75 = 5.625 (£ thousands if Q is in thousands).

formulae.name: Price-discrimination pricing rule
formulae.formula: MR in each market = MC; higher price where PED is lower
formulae.example: Peak commuters (inelastic) pay £30 for a return; off-peak leisure travellers (elastic) pay £15 on the same train route.

applications: Water: England's water companies are regional natural monopolies regulated by Ofwat. Customers cannot switch supplier, so regulation substitutes for competition. Concerns over sewage discharges, under-investment and high debt, especially at Thames Water, which received a record Ofwat penalty of over £120m in 2025, show the risks of monopoly when regulation is weak.

Digital markets: Google has around 90% of UK general search. In 2025 the CMA designated it as having strategic market status under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, allowing conduct requirements such as fair ranking and choice screens. This is a modern response to network effects as a barrier to entry.

Price discrimination on the railways: train operators charge higher peak fares to commuters with inelastic demand and lower off-peak and advance fares to leisure travellers; railcards for 16–25s, seniors and families target groups with more elastic demand. Proof of age or railcard prevents arbitrage.

Pharmaceuticals: patents give around 20 years of legal monopoly. Firms such as AstraZeneca and GSK earn supernormal profits on patented drugs, which fund R&D; once patents expire, generic entry typically cuts prices sharply, illustrating both the static cost and dynamic benefit of monopoly.

Natural monopoly networks: Openreach (part of BT) owns most of the UK's local telephone and broadband lines; Ofcom regulates its wholesale prices and required its legal separation from BT in 2018 so that rival broadband providers get fair access.
evaluation: Economies of scale: if a monopolist's MC and AC are much lower than those of competitive firms, monopoly price can be lower and output higher than under competition, overturning the simple welfare-loss diagram.

Dynamic efficiency: protected supernormal profit can fund innovation (Schumpeter), but secure monopolists may also become complacent; the outcome depends on whether there is a threat of future competition.
Contestability: a monopoly in a contestable market may price close to AC to deter hit-and-run entry, so market share alone exaggerates the harm.
Regulation: natural monopolies cannot be made competitive, so the relevant comparison is regulated monopoly versus nationalisation, not monopoly versus perfect competition.
Price discrimination is not always harmful: it can expand output and access to services, but raises equity concerns when those with inelastic demand are often those with fewest alternatives.

Stakeholders differ: shareholders gain, consumers usually lose, employees may gain job security or lose from lower employment, and suppliers may face buyer power. A judgement should state whose welfare is prioritised.
Time period: monopoly profits often attract innovation that erodes the monopoly (creative destruction), so harms may be temporary in technology markets but persistent in network industries.
misconceptions: Reading price from the MR or MC curve. Output is set where MC = MR, but price is read up to the AR curve at that output.
Drawing MR with the same slope as AR, or hitting the axis at the same point. For a linear AR, MR is twice as steep and meets the quantity axis halfway to AR's intercept.
Saying a monopolist can charge any price it likes. It is constrained by demand: a higher price means lower quantity sold.
Defining price discrimination as charging different prices for different products or where costs differ. It is the same product, with price differences not explained by cost.
Thinking a natural monopoly should simply be forced to charge P = MC. This creates losses because AC is above MC, so a subsidy or average-cost pricing is needed.
exam_tips: Draw MC cutting MR from below, and drop a vertical line from MC = MR up to AR for price and to AC for unit cost; shade (AR – AC) × Q.
For price discrimination questions, state all three conditions and then apply them to the example in the extract (how is the market separated? how is resale prevented?).
In 25-mark essays on monopoly, structure evaluation around stakeholders and dynamic efficiency, and finish with a judgement that depends on barriers, contestability and regulation.
Use the comparison with perfect competition on one diagram to identify consumer surplus transferred and deadweight loss precisely.
When natural monopoly appears in a data response, link it to regulation (Ofwat, Ofgem, Ofcom) and the choice between P = MC with a subsidy and P = AC.

model_answer.question: Evaluate the view that monopolies are always against the public interest. (25 marks)
model_answer.answer:
A monopoly is a market in which one firm dominates supply. In theory it is the only seller; in UK law, a firm with 25% or more of a market can be investigated as having monopoly power. Monopolies are protected by barriers to entry such as economies of scale, patents, network effects and brand loyalty.

The main argument that monopoly harms the public interest is the static welfare loss. Because the monopolist faces the downward-sloping market demand curve, MR lies below AR and is twice as steep for a linear demand curve. The firm maximises profit where MC = MR at Qm and charges Pm from the AR curve. Compared with a competitive industry with the same costs, which would produce Qc at Pc = MC, output is lower and price higher. Part of consumer surplus is transferred to the firm as supernormal profit, (Pm – AC) × Qm, and the triangle between Qm and Qc is a deadweight loss. The monopoly is allocatively inefficient because P > MC, so units that consumers value above their cost of production are not made. Because barriers to entry prevent new firms from competing the profits away, these losses persist into the long run.

Secondly, monopolies may be productively and X-inefficient. There is no competitive pressure forcing the firm to produce at minimum AC, and managers may allow costs to rise through organisational slack. Customers may also suffer poor quality: regional water companies, which customers cannot leave, have been heavily criticised for sewage discharges and under-investment, and Thames Water received a record penalty from Ofwat in 2025.

Thirdly, monopolies may use price discrimination to extract consumer surplus. By separating markets with different elasticities and preventing resale, a firm charges higher prices to consumers with inelastic demand, such as rail commuters at peak times. This raises equity concerns, since those with fewest alternatives pay most.

However, monopolies are not always against the public interest. The most important exception is natural monopoly. Where fixed costs are enormous and LRAC falls over the whole range of market demand, as with water pipes or the electricity grid, one firm can supply the market at a lower average cost than several. Competition would duplicate infrastructure and raise costs. Here the public interest is best served by a regulated monopoly, with the regulator setting prices close to average cost, rather than by trying to create competition.

More generally, economies of scale can mean that a monopolist's MC curve is far below that of a competitive industry. If so, the monopoly's profit-maximising price could be lower and its output higher than the competitive outcome, even after taking a profit margin. The welfare-loss diagram assumes identical costs, which is unrealistic when scale matters.

Monopoly can also promote dynamic efficiency. Supernormal profit provides both the funds and the incentive for research and development. The patent system deliberately grants temporary monopoly for this reason: pharmaceutical firms earn high profits on patented drugs, which finance the next generation of medicines. Without the prospect of monopoly profit, private firms would under-invest in innovation because rivals could copy it immediately.

Price discrimination can also be beneficial. By charging lower prices to groups with elastic demand, firms can serve consumers who would be priced out by a single price, such as students and pensioners, and the extra profit may cross-subsidise loss-making services such as rural rail routes.

Whether a monopoly acts against the public interest therefore depends on several factors. First, whether the market is contestable: if entry is easy, even a single firm may price close to average cost to deter hit-and-run entry. Second, how it is regulated: a monopoly subject to an effective price cap and quality targets can deliver lower prices and investment, while a weakly regulated one can exploit consumers. Third, the time period: in technology markets, monopoly positions are often temporary as innovation creates new competitors, whereas in network industries monopoly is permanent and needs permanent regulation. Fourth, whether the monopoly was gained through innovation or through blocking rivals.

In conclusion, the view is too strong. Unregulated monopolies protected by artificial barriers, with little threat of entry, are likely to act against the public interest through higher prices, deadweight loss and poor quality. But natural monopolies, firms with substantial economies of scale and innovators protected by patents can serve the public interest, provided they are regulated or face the threat of competition. The decisive factor is not market structure alone but whether effective regulation or contestability constrains the firm's behaviour.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge and application: accurate definitions, including the UK 25% threshold, and relevant UK examples (water, rail, pharmaceuticals). Analysis: the full profit-maximisation and welfare-loss chain with reference to both diagrams, plus price discrimination and natural monopoly. Evaluation: several developed counter-arguments (natural monopoly, economies of scale, dynamic efficiency, price discrimination benefits), then explicit 'it depends' factors (contestability, regulation, time, source of monopoly) and a supported final judgement. This meets Level 4 KAA and Level 3 evaluation.

check.q: A monopolist faces AR = 12 – Q. What is its MR?
check.explanation: For a linear AR, MR has the same intercept and twice the slope: MR = 12 – 2Q.

check.q: A profit-maximising monopolist with positive marginal cost will always produce
options: on the inelastic part of its demand curve
where demand is unit elastic
on the elastic part of its demand curve
where AR = AC
check.explanation: MC = MR and MC > 0 means MR > 0, which only happens where PED > 1.

check.q: Which is NOT a condition for successful price discrimination?
options: The firm has price-making power
Markets can be separated and resale prevented
Each group has a different price elasticity of demand
Each group has a different marginal cost of supply
check.explanation: Price discrimination is about different prices for the same product where costs are the same; differences in cost are not required.

check.q: In a natural monopoly, setting price equal to marginal cost leads to
options: supernormal profit
a loss, because AC is above MC
productive efficiency
normal profit
check.explanation: LRAC falls throughout, so LRMC is below LRAC; at P = MC price is below average cost, so the firm makes a loss.

check.q: Under third-degree price discrimination, the higher price is charged in the market where demand is
options: most price elastic
least price elastic
largest
most income elastic
check.explanation: Setting MR = MC in each market gives a higher mark-up where demand is less elastic.

title: Monopsony
overview: A monopsony is a market with a single dominant buyer. Monopsony power appears in labour markets (a dominant local employer, the NHS for many health professions) and in product markets (supermarkets buying from farmers and food manufacturers). The spec asks for the conditions for monopsony, its costs and benefits, and the labour market diagram; the diagram is also needed for wage determination in 3.5.3 and for analysing the minimum wage.
objectives: Define monopsony and explain the conditions in which monopsony power arises
Explain why the marginal cost of labour lies above the supply (average cost of labour) curve
Draw and explain the monopsony labour market diagram, comparing wages and employment with a competitive market
Show how a minimum wage can raise both wages and employment under monopsony
Evaluate the costs and benefits of monopsony for workers, suppliers, firms and consumers

sections.heading: What monopsony is and when it arises
The marginal cost of labour
sections.body:
The key to the monopsony diagram is the difference between the **average cost of labour (ACL)** and the **marginal cost of labour (MCL)**.

The labour supply curve facing the monopsonist slopes upward: to attract more workers it must offer a higher wage. Assuming it cannot wage discriminate, it must pay the **higher wage to all its workers**, not just the new recruit. The supply curve shows the wage paid to each worker, so it is the **average cost of labour (S = ACL)**.

The extra cost of hiring one more worker is therefore the new worker's wage **plus** the increase paid to every existing worker. So **MCL lies above ACL**.

Worked example: a firm employs 10 workers at £500 a week (total wage bill £5,000). To hire an 11th it must raise the wage to £520 for everyone. The new total is 11 × 520 = £5,720. The MCL of the 11th worker is £720, much more than the £520 wage paid to that worker.

If the supply curve is a straight line, W = a + bL, then the total wage bill is aL + bL², and MCL = a + 2bL. So **MCL starts at the same point as the supply curve and is twice as steep**, exactly like the relationship between AR and MR, but rising instead of falling. This is a useful check that your diagram is drawn correctly.

sections.heading: The monopsony labour market diagram
sections.body:
The monopsonist maximises profit by hiring workers up to the point where the **marginal cost of labour equals the marginal revenue product of labour (MCL = MRP)**. The MRP curve is the firm's demand curve for labour (see 3.5.1).

On the diagram:
1. Find employment **Lm** where MCL cuts MRP.
2. Read the wage **down to the supply curve (ACL)** at Lm: this is **Wm**, the lowest wage that will attract Lm workers.

Compare this with a **competitive labour market**, where many employers compete for workers and the wage and employment are set where supply equals demand (S = MRP) at **Wc** and **Lc**.

The monopsonist:
- **employs fewer workers** (Lm < Lc), because each extra worker raises the wage bill for everyone;
- **pays a lower wage** (Wm < Wc);
- pays workers **less than their MRP**: at Lm the MRP of the last worker is well above Wm. The gap is sometimes called **monopsonistic exploitation**; it becomes extra profit for the firm.

There is a **deadweight loss**: workers between Lm and Lc would produce more value (MRP) than the wage they would accept (S), but are not employed. Welfare is transferred from workers to the employer, and some is lost altogether.

The same analysis applies to a **product market monopsony**. Replace labour with, say, milk bought by a supermarket: the supermarket buys less milk than in a competitive market and pays farmers a lower price, below the value of the milk to the supermarket.

sections.heading: Minimum wages and unions under monopsony
sections.body:
Monopsony overturns the standard prediction that a minimum wage reduces employment.

Suppose a **national minimum wage** is set at Wc, the competitive level. The firm can no longer pay less than this. Up to the point where the supply curve reaches the minimum wage, it can hire any number of workers at exactly the NMW. Hiring one more worker no longer requires raising pay for everyone, so the **MCL becomes horizontal at the NMW** up to the supply curve.

The firm now hires where the new MCL (= NMW) meets MRP, at **L2**. Compared with the unregulated monopsony:
- the **wage rises** from W1 to the NMW;
- **employment rises** from L1 to L2;
- monopsony profit falls and the deadweight loss is removed.

If the minimum wage is set **above** the competitive level, employment is determined where the NMW meets MRP: it may still be above the unregulated monopsony level, but at a high enough minimum wage employment falls below L1. So the effect of a minimum wage depends on how much monopsony power exists and how high the minimum is.

A **trade union** has the same effect. By negotiating a single wage for all workers (collective bargaining), it acts as a monopoly seller of labour, countervailing the employer's monopsony power. This is called **bilateral monopoly**: the final wage depends on the relative bargaining power of the two sides and lies somewhere between Wm and the MRP at Lm.

This analysis helps explain evidence from the UK Low Pay Commission that large increases in the National Living Wage since 2016 have not produced the large job losses a competitive model would predict.

sections.heading: Costs and benefits of monopsony
sections.body:
**Costs**
- **Workers**: lower wages and fewer jobs than in a competitive market; wages below MRP. This can increase inequality and in-work poverty.
- **Suppliers**: lower prices and sometimes unfair contract terms. Farmers selling to large supermarkets may face late changes to orders or demands to fund promotions; low prices can make farms unviable and reduce investment. This is why the **Groceries Code Adjudicator** was created in 2013 to enforce the Groceries Supply Code of Practice.
- **Efficiency**: allocative inefficiency and deadweight loss in the input market; under-employment of resources.
- **Long-term supply**: persistently low prices can drive suppliers out, reducing supply, choice and quality in the long run. Low pay in social care, where local authorities are dominant buyers of care services, contributes to staff shortages and high vacancy rates.

**Benefits**
- **Lower costs for the monopsonist**, which may be passed on to consumers as lower prices if the firm faces competition in its selling market. Supermarket buying power is one reason UK food prices have been relatively low compared with incomes; the discounters Aldi and Lidl use strong buying power to keep prices down.
- **Value for money in public services**: the NHS uses its buying power to negotiate lower drug prices than many health systems pay, through NICE assessments and the voluntary pricing scheme with pharmaceutical firms. This saves taxpayers money.
- **Countervailing power**: a monopsony buyer can offset a monopoly seller (for example a large retailer negotiating with a dominant brand), improving the outcome for consumers.
- **Higher profits** may fund investment and expansion.

The overall judgement depends on whether savings are passed on to consumers (which needs competition downstream), how dependent sellers are on the buyer, and whether regulation such as the minimum wage or the Groceries Code limits abuse.

key_terms.definition: A market with a single dominant buyer that can influence the price it pays for a good, service or factor of production.
The ability of a large buyer to pay a lower price than would occur in a competitive market, because sellers have few alternative buyers.
Total wage cost divided by the number of workers; it equals the wage and is shown by the labour supply curve.
The addition to total labour costs from employing one more worker; under monopsony it exceeds the wage because pay rises for all workers.
The extra revenue generated by employing one more worker: marginal physical product × marginal revenue.
A market with a single buyer facing a single seller, such as a monopsony employer bargaining with a trade union.
Market power on one side of a market that offsets market power on the other side.
The UK body set up in 2013 to enforce the Groceries Supply Code of Practice and protect suppliers from unfair treatment by large supermarkets.

diagrams.title: Monopsony in the labour market
diagrams.caption: To hire one more worker the monopsonist must raise the wage for everyone, so MCL lies above (and, with linear supply, is twice as steep as) the supply curve. It hires Lm where MCL = MRP but pays only Wm from the supply curve: fewer workers and a lower wage than the competitive Lc and Wc.

diagrams.title: Minimum wage in a monopsony labour market
diagrams.caption: A minimum wage set at the competitive level makes the marginal cost of labour flat (= NMW) up to the supply curve. The firm now hires L2 where NMW = MRP: both the wage and employment rise, the opposite of the textbook competitive-market prediction.

formulae.name: Marginal cost of labour
formulae.formula: Change in total wage bill ÷ change in number of workers
formulae.example: 10 workers at £500 (£5,000); 11 workers at £520 (£5,720). MCL of the 11th worker = £720.

formulae.name: Linear supply and MCL
formulae.formula: If W = a + bL, MCL = a + 2bL
formulae.example: W = 1 + 0.6L gives MCL = 1 + 1.2L. With MRP = 9 – 0.8L: 1 + 1.2L = 9 – 0.8L, so L = 4 and the wage paid is 1 + 0.6 × 4 = 3.4 (£ per hour, scaled).

formulae.name: Monopsonistic exploitation
formulae.formula: MRP at the chosen employment level – wage paid
formulae.example: MRP of the last worker £5.80, wage £3.40: the gap of £2.40 per hour is captured by the employer.

applications: Supermarkets and farmers: the large UK supermarkets buy a high share of domestic farm output. Dairy farmers have repeatedly protested over milk prices below production cost, and the Groceries Code Adjudicator (2013) has investigated retailers, finding in 2016 that Tesco had seriously breached the Code by delaying payments to suppliers.

The NHS as a monopsony employer: the NHS employs most UK nurses and junior doctors, and national pay scales (Agenda for Change) set pay across the country. This holds down labour costs, but strikes by nurses and resident doctors in 2022–25 and high vacancy rates show the limits of monopsony when workers can emigrate or leave the profession.

The National Living Wage: since 2016 the NLW has risen much faster than average earnings, reaching around two-thirds of median hourly pay in 2024. Low Pay Commission evidence found little sign of large job losses, consistent with employers in low-paid sectors having some monopsony power.

NHS drug purchasing: as the dominant buyer of medicines in the UK, the NHS negotiates prices through NICE appraisals and an agreement with the pharmaceutical industry that caps growth in branded medicine spending, keeping UK drug prices below those in the US.

Globally, cocoa and coffee farmers in West Africa and Latin America often sell to a small number of large traders and processors, receiving a small share of the final retail price; Fairtrade minimum prices are a response to this buyer power.
evaluation: Pass-through: monopsony benefits consumers only if lower input costs lead to lower selling prices, which requires competition in the firm's selling market; a firm that is both monopsonist and monopolist may keep the savings as profit.
Degree of power: workers' or suppliers' ability to switch (mobility, skills, alternative buyers, export markets) determines how far wages or prices can be pushed down.
Long-run supply response: pushing prices too low can drive suppliers out or cause labour shortages (social care, farming), harming the monopsonist itself and consumers through lower quality.
Public versus private monopsony: NHS buying power saves taxpayers money and may be in the public interest, whereas a private employer's monopsony profit is a transfer to shareholders.

Policy response: minimum wages, trade unions and codes of practice can offset monopsony power; under monopsony a moderate minimum wage can raise both pay and employment, but a high one may still cut jobs.
Measurement: monopsony power is hard to observe; economists infer it from how responsive labour supply to individual firms is, so the size of the effect is uncertain.
misconceptions: Reading the wage from the MCL or MRP curve. Employment is set where MCL = MRP, but the wage is read down to the supply (ACL) curve at that employment level.
Drawing MCL parallel to supply. For a linear supply curve, MCL starts at the same intercept and is twice as steep.
Confusing monopsony with monopoly. Monopoly is a single seller; monopsony is a single buyer. A firm can be both in different markets.
Assuming a minimum wage always reduces employment. Under monopsony, a minimum wage up to the competitive level increases employment.
exam_tips: Practise the diagram until it is automatic: S = ACL, MCL twice as steep, MRP = D, employment at MCL = MRP, wage on S. Mark Wc and Lc to show the comparison.
In minimum wage questions, always consider whether the labour market is competitive or monopsonistic; this is a top-band evaluation point.
Use stakeholder analysis for costs and benefits: workers, suppliers, the firm, consumers, taxpayers.
For product-market monopsony (supermarkets), relabel the axes as quantity bought and price paid to suppliers, with the same logic.

model_answer.question: Assess the impact of monopsony power on workers and consumers. (12 marks)
model_answer.answer:
Monopsony power exists when a buyer is large enough to influence the price it pays. In the labour market this means a dominant employer, such as a large employer in a small town or the NHS as the main employer of nurses.

For workers, the main impact is lower wages and fewer jobs. The monopsonist faces an upward-sloping labour supply curve, and to hire one more worker it must raise the wage for all its workers, so the marginal cost of labour lies above the supply curve. It employs where MCL = MRP, at Lm, and pays the wage Wm read from the supply curve. In a competitive market, employment and wages would be set where supply equals MRP at Lc and Wc. So the monopsony employs fewer workers and pays a lower wage, and each worker is paid less than the value of their marginal revenue product. The difference is captured as profit. There is also a deadweight loss, since workers between Lm and Lc would produce more than they would need to be paid. This can increase in-work poverty and inequality.

However, the effect on workers depends on how much power the employer really has. If workers are mobile, with transferable skills and other employers within commuting distance, labour supply to the firm is elastic and the gap between Wm and Wc is small. Policy also matters: a minimum wage set close to the competitive wage makes MCL horizontal at the minimum wage, so the firm employs more workers at a higher wage. This helps explain why the UK's National Living Wage, which has risen to around two-thirds of median pay, has not caused large job losses. Trade unions can provide countervailing power through collective bargaining.

For consumers, monopsony can be beneficial. Lower labour or supplier costs reduce the firm's average and marginal costs. If the firm faces competition in its selling market, these savings are passed on in lower prices. Supermarket buying power over suppliers is one reason UK grocery prices are relatively low, and the NHS uses its buying power to pay less for medicines, benefiting taxpayers.

But this depends on competition downstream. A firm with monopsony power as a buyer and monopoly power as a seller may keep the savings as profit. And in the long run, low wages or supplier prices can reduce supply: low pay in social care, where councils are dominant buyers, has contributed to staff shortages that reduce the quality of care.

Overall, monopsony usually harms workers by lowering wages and employment, but its impact on consumers is ambiguous. Consumers benefit when savings are passed on through competitive selling markets, but may lose if the firm also has selling power or if low prices drive suppliers or workers away. The most important factor is the elasticity of supply to the monopsonist, since this determines how far it can push wages and prices down.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge and application: precise definition, applied to the NHS, supermarkets, NLW and social care. Analysis: a correct chain explaining why MCL > ACL and why employment is set at MCL = MRP with the wage on supply, compared with the competitive outcome. A profit-maximising monopsonist employs labour where
options: the wage equals MRP
MCL equals MRP
supply equals demand
MCL equals the wage

pay a lower wage and employ fewer workers
pay a lower wage and employ more workers

title: Contestability
overview: Contestability shifts the focus from how many firms are in a market to how easily new firms could enter and leave it. Developed by William Baumol in the early 1980s, the theory argues that even a monopoly will behave competitively if the threat of hit-and-run entry is real. It is a powerful evaluation tool for every market structure question and underpins modern competition and regulatory policy.
objectives: Define a contestable market and state the characteristics of a perfectly contestable market
Explain the types of barriers to entry and exit, and distinguish sunk costs from fixed costs
Explain hit-and-run competition and why incumbents in contestable markets earn only normal profit
Draw a diagram contrasting the profit-maximising outcome with the contestable (AR = AC) outcome
Evaluate the implications of contestability for efficiency, firm behaviour and government policy

sections.heading: What makes a market contestable
Barriers to entry and exit
Sunk costs: the crucial barrier
sections.body:
**Sunk costs** are costs that **cannot be recovered** if a firm leaves the market. They are distinct from fixed costs:

- A **fixed cost** does not vary with output in the short run. It may or may not be recoverable.
- A **sunk cost** is lost on exit.

Example: an airline that starts a new route needs aircraft (a large fixed cost). But aircraft can be leased, or sold, or moved to another route, so most of the cost is **not sunk**. By contrast, the advertising campaign to launch the route, staff training specific to that airport and any non-refundable fees are **sunk**.

A water company's pipes, a railway's tunnels or a pharmaceutical firm's R&D spending are almost entirely sunk: they have no alternative use.

Sunk costs matter because they change the **risk of entry**. If an entrant can leave and recover its outlay, entry is low risk: it can enter, take profits while they last, and exit if the incumbent cuts prices. If costs are sunk, an entrant that is driven out by a price war loses them, so it will hesitate to enter. Meanwhile the incumbent's sunk costs are already spent, so it is willing to keep producing at any price above AVC, making a price war a credible threat.

This is why Baumol identified **the absence of sunk costs** as the defining condition of contestability. High sunk costs are the main reason why markets such as utilities, rail infrastructure and telecoms networks are natural monopolies with very low contestability.

sections.heading: Hit-and-run competition and firm behaviour
sections.body:
In a highly contestable market an incumbent earning supernormal profit is vulnerable to **hit-and-run entry**: a new firm enters, undercuts the incumbent, takes the supernormal profit, and exits costlessly when the incumbent responds or the profit disappears.

Because incumbents know this, they have an incentive to behave **as if** they faced competition:
- **Limit pricing at AR = AC.** The diagram contrasts two outcomes for the same firm. If the market were uncontestable, the firm would maximise profit at Qm where MC = MR, charging Pm and earning supernormal profit. In a perfectly contestable market, any price above AC invites entry, so the incumbent sets price close to **Pn, where AR = AC**, earning **normal profit** only and producing a much larger output Qn.
- **Cost minimisation**: an incumbent with costs above the minimum would be undercut by an efficient entrant, so X-inefficiency is driven out and firms have an incentive to be **productively efficient**.
- **Allocative efficiency**: in the limiting case of a perfectly contestable market, price is driven towards marginal and average cost, so P is close to MC.
- **Objectives**: firms may choose to sacrifice short-run profit (revenue or sales maximisation, limit pricing) to protect long-run market position.

Therefore in contestable markets: **normal profit in the long run**, **productive efficiency**, **allocative efficiency** (approximately), **no X-inefficiency**, whatever the number of firms. Even a monopolist in a perfectly contestable market cannot exploit consumers.

Note that the diagram's AR = AC point is on the rising part of AC here; in practice the incumbent may price slightly above AC, as long as the expected profit for an entrant (after its entry costs and the risk of retaliation) is not worth it.

sections.heading: Implications for policy and evaluation
sections.body:
Contestability theory changed how governments approach competition.

**Policy implications:**
- Rather than breaking up large firms, governments can **reduce barriers to entry** and make markets more contestable: deregulation, removing licensing restrictions, opening public-sector contracts to tender, and liberalising markets such as **UK bus services outside London (1986)** and **European aviation (1990s)**.
- Regulators can reduce **sunk costs for entrants** by giving access to existing infrastructure: Ofcom requires Openreach to rent its lines to rival broadband providers; Ofgem allows energy retailers to use the national grid. Separating the natural-monopoly network from the contestable retail activity makes the latter contestable.
- Policies to reduce **switching costs** increase contestability on the demand side: mobile number portability, the Current Account Switch Service, and Open Banking (2018) allowing customers to share data with new financial firms.
- The **CMA** considers barriers to entry when judging whether a merger will substantially lessen competition: a merger in a contestable market is less of a concern.

**Evaluation of the theory:**
- **Perfect contestability is rare.** Almost every market has some sunk costs (advertising, brand building, specific equipment), and incumbents have information and cost advantages.
- **Incumbent response speed**: hit-and-run entry assumes the entrant can enter and leave before the incumbent reacts. In reality incumbents can cut prices within hours (airlines adjust fares in real time), so entrants cannot earn profit before retaliation.
- **Strategic barriers**: incumbents can deliberately raise barriers (exclusive contracts, predatory pricing threats), so contestability can be eroded.
- **Short-run versus long-run**: low-cost airlines made many routes contestable in the 1990s and 2000s, but airport slot constraints at Heathrow and Gatwick now make key routes much less so.
- **Still useful**: the theory explains why some concentrated markets behave competitively and gives policymakers a practical lever (barriers) rather than just structure.

key_terms.definition: A market where there is a credible threat of entry by new firms, because barriers to entry and exit are low.
A market with no barriers to entry or exit, no sunk costs, perfect information and equal access to technology.
A cost that cannot be recovered when a firm leaves a market, such as advertising or specialised equipment with no resale value.
Any factor that makes it difficult for new firms to enter a market and compete on equal terms with incumbents.
A cost of leaving a market, such as sunk costs, redundancy payments or contract penalties, which discourages entry.
Entry by a firm attracted by supernormal profit, which undercuts the incumbent and leaves when profits disappear, recovering its costs.
Setting price at the highest level that deters entry, below the profit-maximising price, often close to average cost.
The costs to a customer of changing supplier, such as time, contract exit fees or loss of loyalty benefits.
Where a product becomes more valuable to each user as more people use it, which can create a strong barrier to entry.

diagrams.title: Contestable market: limit pricing at AR = AC
diagrams.caption: If the market were uncontestable the incumbent would choose Qm and Pm. When entry and exit are costless, any supernormal profit invites hit-and-run entry, so the incumbent prices close to Pn, where AR = AC, earning only normal profit and producing far more.

applications: Low-cost airlines: after EU aviation liberalisation in the 1990s, easyJet and Ryanair entered many European routes. Aircraft could be leased and moved between routes, so sunk costs were low and routes were contestable, forcing incumbents such as British Airways to cut fares. Airport slot shortages at congested airports such as Heathrow now limit this contestability.

Broadband and telecoms: Ofcom requires Openreach to provide wholesale access to its network, so retailers such as Sky, TalkTalk and smaller providers can enter without building their own lines, turning a natural monopoly into a contestable retail market. The growth of alternative fibre networks ('altnets') since around 2020 has increased contestability further.

Open Banking (2018): the CMA required the large banks to let customers share account data securely with authorised third parties, lowering barriers for fintech entrants such as Monzo and Starling and reducing switching costs.

Digital platforms: network effects make search and social media markets very hard to contest despite low marginal costs; this is the reasoning behind the CMA's strategic market status regime from 2024, which aims to keep these markets open to rivals.

UK bus deregulation (1986): outside London, local bus services were opened to competition. Buses are mobile, so sunk costs are low, but in practice large groups often came to dominate local areas, showing that contestability in theory may not produce competition in practice.
evaluation: Number of firms versus threat of entry: a concentrated market may behave competitively if contestable, so concentration ratios alone are a poor guide to consumer welfare.
Speed of incumbent retaliation: if incumbents can cut prices instantly, hit-and-run entry is unprofitable and contestability is weaker than the theory assumes.
Sunk costs are almost always present (brand building, regulatory approval), so contestability is a matter of degree and should be judged market by market.
Incumbents can raise strategic barriers, so contestability is not permanent; regulators need to monitor conduct as well as structure.
Technology can raise or lower contestability: cloud computing lowers capital costs for start-ups, but network effects and data advantages entrench digital incumbents.

Policy implication: improving contestability (access regulation, lower switching costs) can be cheaper and less risky than breaking up firms, but it may not work where natural monopoly cost conditions exist.
misconceptions: Thinking a market with few firms cannot be contestable. Contestability depends on barriers to entry and exit, not the number of incumbents.
Confusing fixed and sunk costs. A fixed cost may be recoverable (a leased aircraft); a sunk cost is lost on exit.
Assuming contestable markets have many firms and are perfectly competitive. A contestable market may have one firm that prices at AC because of the threat of entry.
Ignoring barriers to exit. High exit costs deter entry because entrants consider what they lose if they fail.
exam_tips: Use contestability as an evaluation point in any question on monopoly or oligopoly: 'the harm depends on how contestable the market is'.
When an extract mentions sunk costs, leasing, low capital requirements or new entrants, explicitly link these to contestability and the likely pricing behaviour of incumbents.
Show the contestable outcome on a diagram at AR = AC, contrasted with MC = MR, to demonstrate lower price, higher output and normal profit.
For policy questions, explain how reducing barriers or switching costs can improve outcomes without nationalisation or break-up.

model_answer.question: Discuss the extent to which the threat of entry is likely to keep prices low in markets dominated by one or two firms. (15 marks)
model_answer.answer:
The threat of entry relates to contestability: a market is contestable when barriers to entry and exit are low, so new firms can enter and leave easily. In a perfectly contestable market there are no sunk costs, perfect information and entrants have the same technology as incumbents.

In such a market, even a dominant firm will keep prices low. If the incumbent set the profit-maximising price Pm, where MC = MR, it would earn supernormal profit. Perfect information means potential entrants see the profit, and with no sunk costs they can enter, undercut the incumbent and leave without loss if the incumbent retaliates. This is hit-and-run competition. To avoid it, the incumbent sets a price close to Pn, where AR = AC, earning only normal profit and producing a larger output. It also has an incentive to minimise costs, because an entrant with lower costs could undercut it, so X-inefficiency is reduced. The result resembles a competitive market despite having only one or two firms. For example, after EU aviation liberalisation, many routes with only one or two airlines saw fares fall because low-cost carriers could lease aircraft and move them between routes, so entry was low risk.

However, the extent to which this works depends on sunk costs. Where entry requires spending that cannot be recovered, such as advertising, specialised equipment or infrastructure, entry is risky because a price war could leave the entrant with losses. The incumbent, whose costs are already sunk, can credibly threaten to cut price. Markets such as water supply and rail infrastructure have enormous sunk costs and are effectively uncontestable, so the threat of entry provides no discipline and regulation is needed instead.

It also depends on how quickly incumbents can respond. Hit-and-run entry assumes the entrant can make a profit before the incumbent reacts. In practice airlines and supermarkets can change prices within hours, so an entrant may never make the profit that justified entry. Incumbents can also create strategic barriers, such as loyalty schemes, exclusive supply contracts and heavy branding, that make entry harder.

Finally, some markets have barriers based on network effects. A dominant search engine or social platform is valuable precisely because everyone uses it, so a new firm cannot attract users even with a better product. Here the threat of entry is weak, which is why the CMA introduced the strategic market status regime.

Overall, the threat of entry can keep prices low in dominant-firm markets, but only where sunk costs and switching costs are low and incumbents cannot retaliate instantly. It works best in markets like airline routes with mobile assets, and poorly in network and infrastructure industries. Policymakers can increase its effectiveness by reducing barriers, for example through access regulation of networks and policies that cut switching costs.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: precise definitions of contestability and its conditions. Application: aviation, utilities, digital platforms, CMA policy. Analysis: hit-and-run chain leading to AR = AC pricing and cost minimisation, linked to the diagram. Evaluation: sunk costs, speed of retaliation, strategic barriers and network effects, then a judgement specifying when the threat of entry works and how policy can strengthen it.

title: Demand for labour
overview: Firms do not want workers for their own sake: they want them for what they produce. This lesson explains labour demand as a derived demand, builds the marginal revenue product (MRP) theory of how many workers a firm hires, and analyses what shifts labour demand and what makes it more or less wage elastic. These ideas underpin wage determination, the minimum wage debate and topical issues such as automation and employer National Insurance.
objectives: Explain why the demand for labour is a derived demand
Calculate marginal physical product and marginal revenue product, and explain why MRP eventually falls
Explain why the MRP curve is the firm's demand curve for labour and use MRP = wage to find employment
Analyse the factors that shift the demand for labour
Explain and evaluate the determinants of the elasticity of demand for labour

sections.heading: Labour demand as a derived demand
sections.body:
The demand for labour is a **derived demand**: firms employ workers because of the demand for the **goods and services those workers produce**. Nobody hires a baker for the sake of it; the bakery hires because customers buy bread.

This has important implications:
- If demand for the **product** rises, demand for the labour that produces it rises. Growth in online shopping since the 2010s raised demand for warehouse and delivery workers, while demand for high-street retail staff fell.
- Labour demand is closely linked to the **economic cycle**: in a recession, falling demand for output means falling demand for labour (cyclical unemployment), even if wages do not change.
- The **price of the product** matters: a higher price makes each worker's output more valuable to the firm.
- The **productivity** of labour matters: the more a worker produces, the more the firm is willing to pay.

The demand for labour is also affected by the **cost and availability of other factors of production**, especially capital. Labour and capital can be **substitutes** (self-service checkouts replace cashiers; AI tools replace some routine office tasks) or **complements** (a new delivery van needs a driver; new hospital scanners need radiographers).

The spec focuses on marginal productivity theory, which explains how many workers a profit-maximising firm will hire at a given wage.

sections.heading: Marginal physical product and marginal revenue product
sections.body:
**Marginal physical product (MPP)** is the additional output produced by employing one more worker, holding other factors (capital, land) fixed.

**Marginal revenue product (MRP)** is the additional **revenue** generated by employing one more worker:

**MRP = MPP × MR**

In a perfectly competitive product market MR = P, so MRP = MPP × P.

Because capital is fixed in the short run, the **law of diminishing marginal returns** applies: as more workers are added to the fixed capital, MPP may rise at first (specialisation and teamwork) but eventually falls, because each extra worker has less capital to work with. So MRP eventually falls.

Worked example (product price £10, competitive product market):
- Worker 1: MPP 10 units, MRP £100
- Worker 2: MPP 14 units, MRP £140
- Worker 3: MPP 12 units, MRP £120
- Worker 4: MPP 9 units, MRP £90
- Worker 5: MPP 6 units, MRP £60
- Worker 6: MPP 3 units, MRP £30

If the daily wage is £60, the firm hires workers as long as each one adds at least as much to revenue as to costs. It hires up to the 5th worker, where MRP (£60) = wage (£60). A 6th worker would add £30 to revenue but £60 to costs, reducing profit.

If the firm sells in an imperfectly competitive market, MR falls as output rises, so MRP falls even faster than MPP. This makes labour demand steeper (less elastic) for a firm with market power in its product market.

sections.heading: The MRP curve as the firm's demand curve for labour
sections.body:
A profit-maximising firm hires workers up to the point where **MRP = MCL** (marginal cost of labour). In a **competitive labour market**, the firm is a wage taker: it can hire as many workers as it wants at the market wage, so the supply of labour to the firm is horizontal and **MCL = ACL = wage**. The hiring rule becomes:

**Employ workers until MRP = wage.**

On the first diagram, the horizontal line W = S is the market wage. The firm hires L1, where the falling section of MRP1 cuts the wage. (Where MRP is still rising, an extra worker adds more than the one before, so the firm would always keep hiring past that point.)

Because at each wage the firm hires the quantity where MRP equals that wage, the **downward-sloping part of the MRP curve is the firm's demand curve for labour**. A higher wage moves the firm **along** its MRP curve to lower employment.

The **market (industry) demand for labour** is found by adding horizontally the demand curves of all firms that employ that type of labour.

Marginal productivity theory has limitations:
- MRP is very hard to **measure** for many workers, especially in teams or in the public sector (what is the MRP of a nurse or a teacher?).
- Wages are often set by **collective bargaining**, pay scales or custom rather than at MRP.
- Employers with **monopsony power** pay less than MRP (see 3.4.6).
- It assumes firms are profit maximisers with full information.

Even so, it gives a clear, testable prediction: other things equal, workers whose output is more valuable are paid more.

sections.heading: Shifts in the demand for labour
sections.body:
A change in the wage causes a movement along the demand curve. A change in any other factor that changes MRP at every level of employment **shifts the demand curve**.

The demand for labour shifts **right** (MRP2 on the first diagram) when:
- **demand for the final product rises**, raising its price (MR) and so MRP. Rising demand for healthcare as the population ages increases demand for care workers and nurses.
- **labour productivity increases** (higher MPP) through better training, education, management or complementary capital.
- **the price of complementary capital falls** or new technology complements labour.
- **the price of substitute capital rises**, making labour relatively cheaper.
- **non-wage costs of employment fall**, such as employer National Insurance contributions (NICs), pension contributions or regulatory costs.

It shifts **left** when the opposite occurs: a fall in product demand (recession), falling productivity, cheaper substitute technology (automation and AI) or higher non-wage costs.

A topical example: from April 2025 the rate of employer NICs rose from 13.8% to 15% and the threshold at which employers start paying fell from £9,100 to £5,000 a year. This raised the cost of employing each worker, especially part-time and low-paid workers, at the same time as the National Living Wage rose. Business surveys in 2025 reported reduced hiring, particularly in retail and hospitality, consistent with a fall in labour demand or a movement along the demand curve as the total cost of employment rose.

sections.heading: Elasticity of demand for labour
sections.body:
The **wage elasticity of demand for labour** measures how responsive the quantity of labour demanded is to a change in the wage:

**% change in quantity of labour demanded ÷ % change in the wage**

The second diagram shows that the same wage rise (W1 to W2) causes a large fall in employment when demand is elastic but only a small fall when demand is inelastic. Labour demand is **more elastic** when:

- **Labour is easy to substitute with capital or other labour.** Routine tasks (checkout work, data entry, warehouse picking) can be automated, so demand is elastic. Highly skilled or creative work is harder to substitute.
- **Labour costs are a large proportion of total costs.** In labour-intensive industries such as social care and hospitality, a wage rise has a big effect on costs and prices, so employment responds more. Where labour is a small share of costs (oil refining), demand is inelastic.
- **Demand for the final product is price elastic.** If higher wages are passed on in higher prices and consumers switch away easily, output and employment fall sharply. This is why labour demand is elastic in internationally competitive industries.
- **The time period is long.** In the short run firms cannot easily replace workers with machines; over time they can redesign production, so labour demand becomes more elastic.
- **Supply of substitute factors is elastic**, so they can be obtained easily if labour becomes more expensive.

Why this matters: if labour demand is **inelastic**, trade unions and minimum wages can raise pay with little loss of jobs. If it is **elastic**, wage rises cause significant job losses or automation. This is a central evaluation point in debates about the National Living Wage.

key_terms.definition: Demand for a factor of production that arises from the demand for the goods or services it helps to produce.
The additional output produced by employing one more worker, other factors held constant.
The additional revenue generated by employing one more worker: MPP × MR.
As more of a variable factor is added to a fixed factor, the marginal product of the variable factor eventually falls.
The theory that a profit-maximising firm employs workers up to the point where the MRP of labour equals the marginal cost of labour, which in a competitive labour market is the wage.

key_terms.term: Wage elasticity of demand for labour
key_terms.definition: The responsiveness of the quantity of labour demanded to a change in the wage rate.
Costs of employing workers other than wages, such as employer National Insurance, pension contributions and training costs.

diagrams.title: MRP and the firm's demand for labour
diagrams.caption: MRP = MPP × MR. After a point diminishing returns make MRP fall, and the falling part is the firm's labour demand curve. A wage-taking firm hires until MRP = wage (L1). A rise in the product's price raises MRP at every level of employment (MRP2), so the firm hires L2.

diagrams.title: Elastic versus inelastic demand for labour
diagrams.caption: The same wage rise from W1 to W2 cuts employment from L1 to Le when labour demand is elastic, but only to Li when it is inelastic (labour hard to substitute, small share of costs, inelastic product demand).

formulae.name: Marginal revenue product
formulae.formula: MRP = MPP × MR (= MPP × P in a competitive product market)
formulae.example: A worker adds 12 units a day, each sold for £8: MRP = 12 × £8 = £96 per day.

formulae.name: Hiring rule (competitive labour market)
formulae.formula: Employ until MRP = wage
formulae.example: MRPs of £140, £120, £90, £60, £30 for workers 2–6 and a wage of £60: hire 5 workers.

formulae.name: Wage elasticity of demand for labour
formulae.formula: % change in quantity of labour demanded ÷ % change in wage
formulae.example: Wage rises 8%, employment falls 2%: elasticity = –2 ÷ 8 = –0.25, inelastic.

applications: Employer National Insurance: the April 2025 rise in employer NICs from 13.8% to 15%, with the threshold cut to £5,000, increased the non-wage cost of employment. Combined with a 6.7% rise in the National Living Wage the same month, it raised the total cost of employing low-paid workers, and surveys reported reduced hiring in labour-intensive sectors such as hospitality and retail.

Automation in retail: self-service checkouts and automated warehouses substitute for routine labour. As the cost of this technology falls relative to wages, demand for checkout staff falls and labour demand in these jobs becomes more elastic.

Ageing population and care: rising demand for adult social care increases the derived demand for care workers. Because care is labour intensive and hard to automate, demand for care workers is relatively wage inelastic.

Generative AI: tools that draft text and code may substitute for some entry-level professional tasks while complementing others, raising the productivity (and so MRP) of workers who use them well; the overall effect on labour demand is still uncertain.

Globally, rising wages in coastal China since the 2000s pushed labour-intensive manufacturing such as clothing towards lower-wage economies like Bangladesh and Vietnam, showing that labour demand is elastic in footloose industries with price-elastic product demand.
evaluation: Measurement of MRP: for many jobs, especially in services, teams and the public sector, individual MRP cannot be measured, so marginal productivity theory explains broad patterns rather than individual pay.
Market power: firms with product-market power (MR < P) and labour-market power (monopsony) will not hire where wage = P × MPP, so real outcomes differ from the competitive model.
Elasticity varies over time: in the short run employment may hardly respond to wage rises, but in the long run firms automate or relocate, so the full effect of a wage or tax change takes years.
Substitutes versus complements: technology can reduce or increase labour demand depending on whether it replaces tasks or raises workers' productivity; the net effect depends on the type of job.
Derived demand ties labour markets to the macroeconomy: in a recession labour demand falls regardless of wage levels, so wage cuts may not restore employment if product demand is weak.
misconceptions: Thinking a rise in the wage shifts the demand for labour. It causes a movement along the MRP curve; only changes in productivity, product price or other factors shift it.
Using total or average product instead of marginal product. The hiring decision depends on the extra output and revenue from the last worker.
Assuming MRP = MPP × P always. This only holds in a competitive product market; with market power, MRP = MPP × MR, which is lower.
Treating the rising part of the MRP curve as part of labour demand. Firms hire where the falling part of MRP equals the wage.
exam_tips: Calculate MPP and MRP in a table carefully in short-answer questions: MPP is the change in total output; MRP is MPP × MR.
Label the diagram fully: MRP = D for labour, horizontal wage line labelled W = ACL = MCL for a competitive labour market.
When asked about the effect of a minimum wage or union wage rise, use the determinants of labour demand elasticity to judge the size of any job losses.
Link to current data: NICs, the NLW, automation and AI give strong application for Paper 1 and Paper 3.

model_answer.question: Explain two factors that might cause the demand for care workers to be wage inelastic, and assess the likely effect of a large rise in their wages on employment. (12 marks)
model_answer.answer:
The wage elasticity of demand for labour measures the responsiveness of the quantity of labour demanded to a change in the wage. Demand for labour is a derived demand: care homes employ workers because of the demand for care services.

The first factor making demand for care workers inelastic is that they are difficult to substitute with capital. Personal care, such as helping residents wash and eat, requires human contact and judgement, so it cannot easily be automated. If wages rise, care providers cannot switch to machines, so they continue employing almost as many workers and employment falls only slightly.

The second factor is that demand for the final product, care, is price inelastic. Care is a necessity for people who can no longer live independently, and the number of elderly people is rising. Even if higher wages are passed on in higher fees, demand for care falls only a little, so the derived demand for care workers falls only a little.

On a diagram, an inelastic MRP curve means that a rise in the wage from W1 to W2 causes only a small fall in employment from L1 to Li, compared with a large fall if demand were elastic.

However, a key factor pushes the other way: labour costs are a very large share of total costs in care homes, often more than half. A large wage rise therefore raises total costs substantially. Many care homes rely on fees paid by local authorities, which are themselves under financial pressure, so they may not be able to pass on the costs. In that case providers may reduce staffing ratios, close homes or reduce hours, making the effect on employment larger than the inelastic factors suggest. The April 2025 rise in employer National Insurance alongside the National Living Wage increase showed this pressure, with care providers warning of closures.

The time period also matters. In the short run, providers have little choice but to keep staff; in the long run, they may invest in technology such as monitoring systems that reduce night staffing, so demand becomes more elastic.

Moreover, the care sector suffers from staff shortages and high vacancy rates, suggesting that at current wages employers are struggling to recruit. If care providers have some monopsony power, a higher wage could even raise employment by attracting workers into the sector.

Overall, a large wage rise is likely to cause only a small fall in employment in the short run, because care workers are hard to replace and demand for care is inelastic. The overall effect depends mainly on who funds the extra cost: if the government increases funding to local authorities, employment may be maintained or even rise; if providers must absorb the cost, closures could make job losses significant.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: correct definitions of derived demand and wage elasticity of labour demand. Application: consistently applied to care, including NICs and NLW. Analysis: two clear factors each with a chain to employment, supported by a diagram reference.
