title: Supply of labour
overview: The supply of labour is the number of workers (or hours) willing and able to work in an occupation at each wage. This lesson covers individual and market labour supply, wage and non-wage factors, the elasticity of labour supply, and the geographical and occupational immobility of labour, which explain why labour shortages and unemployment can exist side by side. These concepts are essential for explaining wage differentials and for evaluating labour market policy.
objectives: Explain the individual labour supply decision, including the income and substitution effects and the backward-bending supply curve
Distinguish wage factors (movements along the supply curve) from non-wage factors (shifts in supply)
Analyse the factors that shift the market supply of labour to an occupation
Explain the determinants of the elasticity of labour supply
Explain geographical and occupational immobility of labour and evaluate policies to reduce it

sections.heading: The individual's supply of labour
sections.body:
Each individual chooses how to divide their time between **work** (which earns income) and **leisure**. The wage is the price of leisure: every hour not worked means giving up the hourly wage.

When the wage rises, two effects pull in opposite directions:
- **Substitution effect**: leisure becomes more expensive relative to work (each hour of leisure costs more forgone income), so the individual substitutes work for leisure and **works more hours**.
- **Income effect**: the individual is now better off and can earn the same income by working fewer hours. If leisure is a normal good, they will want more of it, so they **work fewer hours**.

At **low wages** the substitution effect usually dominates, so the supply curve slopes upward: higher wages mean more hours. At **high wages** the income effect may dominate: a worker earning a high hourly rate may choose to work fewer hours and enjoy more leisure. This gives the **backward-bending individual labour supply curve** shown on the first diagram: hours rise with the wage up to W* and then fall.

The backward bend is relevant to policy. For example, some senior NHS doctors reduced their extra hours when pension tax rules meant additional earnings triggered large tax charges; the effective wage for extra hours fell and the income effect was already strong. These rules were relaxed in 2023 partly to address this.

In practice many workers cannot choose their hours freely, because contracts set hours, but they can choose part-time versus full-time work, overtime, second jobs or early retirement.

sections.heading: Market supply: wage and non-wage factors
sections.body:
The **market supply of labour** to an occupation is the total number of workers willing and able to work in it at each wage. Even if some individuals' supply bends backwards, market supply normally **slopes upward**, because a higher wage attracts **new workers** into the occupation from other jobs, from unemployment or from outside the labour force.

A **change in the wage** of the occupation causes a **movement along** its supply curve.

A change in any **non-wage factor** **shifts** the supply curve. Supply to an occupation increases (shifts right) when:
- **Non-monetary benefits improve**: job satisfaction, status, flexibility (hybrid working), job security, holidays, pensions, working conditions, training and promotion prospects.
- **Wages in alternative occupations fall**, making this job relatively more attractive.
- **Barriers to entry fall**: shorter qualification requirements, fewer licensing rules.
- **The working population grows**: net migration, higher participation by women or older workers, a larger cohort of school leavers.
- **Government policy** changes incentives: lower income tax, changes to benefits, more childcare support (which raises the participation of parents).
- **Education and training** increase the number of people qualified for the job.

Supply shifts **left** when these factors move the other way. The second diagram shows a fall in supply from S1 to S2, for example because a job becomes more stressful, or because tighter immigration rules reduce the number of overseas recruits: the wage rises from W1 to W2 but employment falls from L1 to L2.

UK examples: the post-2021 shortage of HGV drivers reflected poor working conditions, an ageing workforce and fewer EU drivers after Brexit; wages rose sharply in response. After 2022 the UK saw a rise in economic inactivity due to long-term sickness, which reduced labour supply.

sections.heading: Elasticity of labour supply
sections.body:
The **wage elasticity of supply of labour** measures how responsive the quantity of labour supplied to an occupation is to a change in the wage:

**% change in quantity of labour supplied ÷ % change in the wage**

Labour supply is **more elastic** when:
- **Little skill or training is needed**: unskilled jobs (shelf-stacking, cleaning, bar work) can be filled quickly from a large pool of potential workers when wages rise.
- **The time period is long**: in the long run, people can train and qualify for skilled occupations. In the short run the supply of doctors or airline pilots is very inelastic because qualification takes years.
- **There is spare labour**: high unemployment or many people outside the labour force who could be attracted back.
- **Workers are mobile**, geographically and occupationally.
- **Vocation and job satisfaction are low**: workers in jobs with strong vocational attachment (nursing, teaching) may not leave quickly if pay falls, making supply less responsive in the short run.

Why it matters: when demand for a type of labour rises, **inelastic supply** means a large wage rise and small employment rise (doctors, specialist software engineers, premier league footballers), while **elastic supply** means employment rises with little wage pressure (warehouse workers in areas with available labour). This is a central explanation of **wage differentials**: occupations with inelastic supply and high demand command high wages.

For macroeconomics, inelastic labour supply means that rising labour demand causes wage-push inflation rather than higher employment, which is why the Bank of England monitors labour market tightness closely.

sections.heading: Immobility of labour
Migration and the labour supply
sections.body:
Migration has a direct effect on labour supply. Net inward migration shifts the supply of labour to the right, particularly in sectors that rely on migrant workers such as health and social care, hospitality, agriculture and construction.

Key UK developments:
- After the end of free movement with the EU in 2021, the UK introduced a points-based immigration system. Sectors that relied on EU workers, such as food processing and hospitality, reported shortages, reducing labour supply in those markets and pushing up wages.
- Net migration then rose to record levels, roughly 900,000 in the year to mid-2023, driven largely by non-EU workers in health and care and by students. Tighter rules from 2024, such as restrictions on care-worker dependants and higher salary thresholds for skilled worker visas, contributed to a sharp fall in net migration during 2024–25.

Economic effects to analyse:
- **Supply side**: migration increases labour supply, can fill skills shortages and raises potential output.
- **Wages**: in sectors where migrant labour is a close substitute for existing workers, increased supply may moderate wage growth; most UK studies find small overall effects on average wages, with slightly larger effects at the low-paid end.
- **Demand side**: migrants also spend, raising demand for labour across the economy, so the effect on unemployment is generally small.

This is a good synoptic link to 2.1.3 and to the macroeconomic effects of labour supply on growth and inflation.

key_terms.definition: The number of workers, or hours of work, offered in an occupation at each wage rate over a period.
A higher wage raises the opportunity cost of leisure, so individuals substitute work for leisure and supply more hours.
A higher wage raises income, so individuals can afford more leisure and may supply fewer hours.
An individual labour supply curve that slopes upward at low wages and bends backward at high wages, when the income effect outweighs the substitution effect.

Influences on labour supply other than the occupation's wage, such as working conditions, job satisfaction, training, barriers to entry and the size of the working population; they shift the supply curve.
The responsiveness of the quantity of labour supplied to a change in the wage rate.
Difficulty in moving between different jobs because of lack of skills, qualifications or experience.
Difficulty in moving between areas to take up work, because of housing costs, family ties or lack of information.
People of working age who are neither employed nor actively seeking work, such as students, carers and the long-term sick.

diagrams.title: Individual labour supply: the backward-bending curve
diagrams.caption: At low wages the substitution effect dominates: leisure becomes more expensive, so hours rise. Above W* the income effect dominates: the worker is rich enough to buy more leisure, so hours fall as the wage rises.

diagrams.title: A fall in labour supply to an occupation
diagrams.caption: A worsening of a non-wage factor (e.g. more stressful conditions) or tighter entry requirements shifts supply left from S1 to S2: the wage rises to W2 and employment falls to L2.

formulae.name: Wage elasticity of labour supply
formulae.formula: % change in quantity of labour supplied ÷ % change in wage
formulae.example: Wages for HGV drivers rise 15% and the number of drivers available rises 3% in the first year: elasticity = 3 ÷ 15 = 0.2, inelastic.

applications: HGV drivers: in 2021 a shortage of roughly 100,000 drivers, linked to poor conditions, an ageing workforce, Covid-related testing backlogs and the departure of EU drivers, caused fuel and supermarket supply problems. Driver pay rose sharply and the government expanded testing and training, illustrating inelastic short-run supply and the role of non-wage factors.

Economic inactivity: after the pandemic, UK inactivity due to long-term sickness rose to around 2.8 million people, reducing labour supply and contributing to labour shortages and wage pressure in 2022–23.

Childcare support: the expansion of funded childcare hours for working parents in England from 2024–25 aims to increase labour supply by raising participation, especially among mothers of young children.

Geographical immobility: average house prices in London are roughly three times those in the North East, so a worker from a low-cost region faces a large rise in housing costs to take a better-paid London job, limiting mobility even when vacancies exist.
Globally, Gulf states rely heavily on migrant labour from South Asia, showing how migration can make labour supply highly elastic in sectors such as construction.
evaluation: Income versus substitution effects: whether a wage rise increases hours depends on which effect dominates, so tax cuts or pay rises do not always raise labour supply, especially for high earners.
Time period: labour supply to skilled occupations is very inelastic in the short run but more elastic in the long run as people train, so wage premiums for shortages may be temporary.
Non-wage factors are often as important as pay: improving conditions or flexibility can raise supply without large wage rises, as public-sector employers have tried.
Immobility policies take time and are uncertain: retraining older workers may have low returns, and housing supply responds slowly to planning reform.
Migration effects depend on skills and sectors: inflows can fill shortages and raise output, but effects on wages differ between groups and are contested.
misconceptions: Saying a higher wage shifts the supply of labour. It causes a movement along the supply curve; non-wage factors shift it.
Assuming higher wages always increase hours worked. The income effect can outweigh the substitution effect at high wages.
Confusing the individual backward-bending curve with market supply. Market supply to an occupation usually slopes upward because higher wages attract new workers.
Treating occupational and geographical immobility as the same. They have different causes and need different policies.
exam_tips: When an extract describes a shortage, use both non-wage factors (shifts) and elasticity (time to train) to explain why wages rise.
Draw a supply shift diagram and state what happens to both the wage and employment.
For policy questions on immobility, match the policy to the type of immobility and evaluate cost, time lag and effectiveness.
Use income and substitution effects to evaluate the impact of income tax changes on labour supply, linking to 4.5.2.

model_answer.question: Assess the factors that may explain why there are persistent shortages of some types of skilled workers in the UK. (15 marks)
model_answer.answer:
A labour shortage exists when the demand for workers in an occupation exceeds the supply at the current wage, shown by persistent vacancies. Skilled occupations such as nurses, engineers, HGV drivers and specialist software developers have experienced shortages in recent years.

The first factor is the inelastic supply of skilled labour in the short run. Becoming a nurse or an engineer requires years of training and qualifications, so when demand rises the number of qualified workers cannot increase quickly. On a labour market diagram, an increase in demand with inelastic supply causes a large rise in the wage but only a small rise in employment. If wages are not allowed to rise, for example because they are set by national pay scales, the result is persistent vacancies. In the NHS, pay is set through national pay bodies and has at times fallen in real terms, so the wage has not risen enough to clear the market.

The second factor is occupational immobility. Workers in declining industries may lack the skills to move into shortage occupations, and retraining is costly and time consuming, especially for older workers. So unemployment in some occupations can coexist with vacancies in others.

Thirdly, geographical immobility matters. Many skilled jobs are concentrated in London and the South East, where housing costs are very high. Workers in other regions may not move even when jobs are available, so local shortages persist.

Fourthly, non-wage factors can reduce supply. HGV driving involves long hours, time away from home and poor facilities, contributing to a shortage of around 100,000 drivers in 2021. Stress and workload have caused some nurses and teachers to leave their professions, shifting labour supply left.

Finally, migration policy matters. The end of free movement with the EU in 2021 reduced the inflow of workers in sectors such as haulage and care, shifting supply left.

However, the importance of these factors varies. The time-to-train explanation suggests shortages should ease in the long run as wages rise and more people train, and HGV shortages did ease after 2022 as pay rose and testing capacity increased. Persistent shortages are therefore more likely where wages are prevented from adjusting, as in public-sector occupations with national pay scales and monopsony employers, than in private-sector markets where wages can rise. Similarly, migration rules were relaxed for health and care visas, so the effect of Brexit on supply has been partly offset in some sectors.

Overall, the main explanation for persistent shortages is the combination of inelastic short-run supply due to long training periods with wages that do not adjust, especially in the public sector. Immobility and non-wage factors add to the problem, but the most persistent shortages are found where the price mechanism is weakest. The solution therefore depends on the sector: higher pay and better conditions where the state is the dominant employer, and investment in training and housing supply where immobility is the main cause.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge and application: shortage defined and applied to nurses, HGV drivers and engineers. Analysis: separate, developed chains for elasticity, occupational and geographical immobility, non-wage factors and migration, with diagram reference. Evaluation: weighs time period, wage flexibility, monopsony and policy changes, and reaches a judgement that identifies the key cause and its implications.

title: Wage determination
overview: This lesson brings labour demand and supply together to explain how wages are set in competitive and non-competitive labour markets. It covers wage differentials, the influence of trade unions, monopsony employers and government, and the economics of the National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage. Expect 15- and 25-mark questions on the minimum wage that require you to use both the competitive and the monopsony diagram.
objectives: Explain wage determination in a competitive labour market using demand (MRP) and supply
Explain why wage differentials exist between occupations, regions, genders and skill levels
Explain wage determination in non-competitive markets: monopsony, trade unions and bilateral monopoly
Analyse the effects of the National Minimum Wage in competitive and monopsony labour markets
Evaluate government intervention in labour markets, including public-sector pay and maximum wages

sections.heading: Wages in a competitive labour market
sections.body:
A **perfectly competitive labour market** has many employers and many workers, homogeneous labour, perfect information, and free movement of workers between jobs. No individual employer or worker can influence the wage: all are wage takers.

The market wage is determined where **market demand for labour (the sum of firms' MRP curves) equals market supply**. At any wage above equilibrium there is excess supply (unemployment in that occupation), which pushes wages down; below it there is excess demand (vacancies), which pushes wages up.

In this model:
- each firm hires until **MRP = wage**, so workers are paid the value of their marginal revenue product;
- the wage changes when demand or supply shifts. A rise in demand for the product, higher productivity or cheaper complementary capital shifts demand right, raising wages and employment. A fall in supply (worse conditions, tighter migration rules) raises wages but cuts employment.

The competitive model gives the simplest explanation of **wage differentials**: occupations differ in demand and supply conditions.
- **High wages** arise where MRP is high (the product is valuable and workers are productive) and supply is limited and inelastic (long training, rare talent): surgeons, senior software engineers, top footballers.
- **Low wages** arise where MRP is low and supply is plentiful and elastic (few skills needed): cleaners, care assistants, retail staff.

The **elasticity of supply** shapes what happens when demand changes. With inelastic supply, extra demand is reflected mainly in higher wages: an economic rent. Premier League players' pay rose dramatically as broadcasting revenue (and so their MRP) rose, because the supply of elite players is almost perfectly inelastic.

sections.heading: Explaining wage differentials
sections.body:
Real-world wage differences have several causes. A strong answer distinguishes market forces from imperfections.

**Market (competitive) explanations**
- **Skills, qualifications and productivity**: higher MRP and restricted supply. Graduates earn a premium over non-graduates on average.
- **Compensating differentials**: unpleasant, dangerous or unsociable jobs (offshore oil rigs, night shifts) must pay more to attract workers; jobs with high non-monetary rewards may pay less.
- **Regional differences**: higher living costs and stronger demand in London explain London weighting and higher average pay.
- **Product demand**: wages are higher in growing, profitable industries such as tech and finance.

**Non-competitive explanations**
- **Monopsony power**: employers with buying power pay below MRP.
- **Trade unions**: unionised workers may earn a wage premium.
- **Discrimination**: if employers undervalue certain groups, those groups are paid less than their MRP or are excluded from higher-paid jobs (occupational segregation). The UK gender pay gap for full-time employees was around 7% in 2024, and larger for all employees because women are more likely to work part time. Causes include discrimination, caring responsibilities and part-time work (the 'motherhood penalty'), and occupational segregation.
- **Government**: minimum wages, public-sector pay review bodies, equal pay legislation (Equality Act 2010) and gender pay gap reporting for employers with 250+ staff.
- **Imperfect information and immobility**: workers may not know about better-paid jobs or cannot move to them.
- **Status, custom and bargaining power**: executive pay is partly set by remuneration committees and comparisons rather than measurable MRP, which raises principal-agent questions.

sections.heading: Trade unions and bilateral monopoly
sections.body:
A **trade union** is an organisation of workers that bargains collectively with employers over pay and conditions. Around a fifth of UK employees are union members, much higher in the public sector than in the private sector.

**In a competitive labour market**, a union that negotiates a wage above equilibrium acts like a minimum wage (first diagram). The wage rises for those employed, but firms move up their MRP curve and employ fewer workers (Ld), while more workers want jobs at the higher wage (Ls). The union trades off **higher pay for members in work** against **fewer jobs**. The size of the job loss depends on the **elasticity of demand for labour**: unions are most effective where demand is inelastic, for example where workers are hard to replace or labour is a small share of costs. Unions may also try to **shift demand** right (productivity deals, campaigns for public spending) or **restrict supply** (closed shops, now illegal; longer training requirements), which raises wages without the same job losses.

**In a monopsony labour market**, a union can raise wages **and** employment. The monopsonist pays below the competitive wage and employs below the competitive level. A union bargaining for a single wage makes the firm's MCL horizontal at that wage up to the supply curve, just as a minimum wage does, so employment can rise towards the competitive level. When a single dominant employer faces a single union, the market is a **bilateral monopoly**: the outcome depends on bargaining power, and lies between the monopsony wage and the MRP of the last worker employed.

**Union power** depends on: membership levels and solidarity; the elasticity of demand for labour; the employer's profitability; public support; and the law. UK law requires secret ballots before strikes, and since 2017 a turnout of at least 50% (with extra thresholds in important public services). The Strikes (Minimum Service Levels) Act 2023 added further limits, and the Labour government's Employment Rights Bill, introduced in 2024, included its repeal.

Unions may also improve productivity by giving workers a 'voice', reducing staff turnover and training costs.

sections.heading: The National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage
sections.body:
The **National Minimum Wage (NMW)** was introduced in 1999. Since 2016 the top rate is called the **National Living Wage (NLW)**, which applied from age 25, then 23 (2021) and 21 (April 2024). It rose to £12.21 an hour in April 2025 and £12.71 in April 2026. The Low Pay Commission recommends rates, and the NLW reached its target of **two-thirds of median hourly earnings** in 2024.

**Competitive labour market analysis** (first diagram). A minimum wage above the market-clearing wage We:
- raises pay for those who keep their jobs;
- reduces employment from Le to Ld as firms move up their MRP curve;
- increases the quantity of labour supplied to Ls;
- creates **excess supply (unemployment)** of Ls – Ld.
The job loss is greater where labour demand is elastic (labour-intensive, internationally competitive or easily automated jobs) and where the minimum is set far above the market wage.

**Monopsony analysis** (second diagram). The unregulated monopsonist employs L1 at W1. A minimum wage at the competitive level makes MCL horizontal at the NMW up to the supply curve. The firm hires L2 where NMW = MRP: **both wages and employment rise**.

**Other effects to consider:**
- **Reduced poverty and inequality** for the low paid, although many low-paid workers live in households with other earners, so the NMW is less precisely targeted than benefits.
- **Incentives**: higher pay makes work more attractive than benefits, raising labour supply and participation.
- **Productivity**: higher pay may boost morale and reduce staff turnover (efficiency wage effects), and may push firms to invest and train, raising MRP.
- **Costs and prices**: firms may pass on costs in higher prices, cut hours, reduce non-wage benefits or squeeze pay differentials above the minimum.
- **Regional effects**: one national rate bites harder in lower-wage regions where median pay is lower.
- **Government finances**: higher pay raises tax revenue and reduces spending on in-work benefits.

Evidence from the Low Pay Commission and academic studies has generally found **small or negligible employment effects** from UK minimum wage increases, consistent with monopsony power and productivity responses. Whether this continues at higher levels relative to median pay is uncertain, especially combined with the 2025 rise in employer National Insurance.

sections.heading: Other government intervention in labour markets
sections.body:
**Public-sector pay**. The government is the dominant employer of nurses, teachers, doctors, police and armed forces. Pay is recommended by independent **pay review bodies** and decided by the government, so it reflects budget constraints and political choices as well as market forces. Holding public-sector pay down below private-sector pay (real cuts in the 2010s and during the 2022 inflation surge) led to recruitment and retention problems and strikes by nurses, resident doctors, teachers and rail workers in 2022–24. The government is effectively a monopsony employer: it can hold wages down in the short run, but labour supply responds in the long run as workers leave or emigrate.

**Maximum wages** are rarely used, but there are pay ratios and caps: the EU bonus cap on bankers (two times salary), removed by the UK in 2023, and limits on executive pay in some public bodies. Arguments for: reducing inequality, addressing executive pay set without regard to MRP. Arguments against: loss of talent to other countries, pay shifting into other forms, reduced incentives.

**Policies on discrimination**: equal pay laws, gender pay gap reporting, flexible working rights and shared parental leave aim to reduce non-market wage differentials.

**Policies on supply and mobility**: training, apprenticeships, childcare and migration rules (see 3.5.2).

**Overall**, government intervention can correct labour market failures such as monopsony power, discrimination and information gaps, but may cause government failure: minimum wages that are set too high can price low-productivity workers out of jobs, and public-sector pay restraint can create shortages that reduce the quality of services.

key_terms.definition: A labour market with many employers and workers, homogeneous labour, perfect information and mobility, in which all are wage takers and the wage is set by supply and demand.
A difference in wage rates between workers in different occupations, industries, regions or groups.
Extra pay required to attract workers into jobs with unpleasant, risky or unsociable conditions.
An organisation of workers that negotiates collectively with employers over pay and working conditions.
Negotiation of pay and conditions between an employer and a trade union representing a group of workers.
A labour market where a monopsony employer bargains with a monopoly seller of labour, such as a trade union; the wage depends on relative bargaining power.
A legal minimum hourly wage that employers must pay; the top rate in the UK is called the National Living Wage.
Earnings above the minimum needed to keep a worker in their current job (transfer earnings).
The minimum payment needed to keep a worker in their current occupation, equal to what they could earn in their next best alternative.
A wage above the market level paid to raise worker productivity by improving motivation and reducing staff turnover.

diagrams.title: Minimum wage in a competitive labour market
diagrams.caption: A minimum wage above the market-clearing We raises the wage for those in work, but firms cut employment to Ld while more people want work (Ls): excess supply Ls – Ld. A trade union that negotiates a wage above We has the same effect.

diagrams.title: Minimum wage in a monopsony labour market
diagrams.caption: A minimum wage set at the competitive level makes the marginal cost of labour flat (= NMW) up to the supply curve. The firm now hires L2 where NMW = MRP: both the wage and employment rise, the opposite of the textbook competitive-market prediction.

formulae.name: Unemployment created by a minimum wage (competitive model)
formulae.formula: Quantity of labour supplied at NMW – quantity demanded at NMW
formulae.example: At a minimum wage of £12, 7,140 workers want jobs but firms want 3,750: excess supply = 3,390 workers.

formulae.name: Minimum wage bite
formulae.formula: Minimum wage ÷ median hourly earnings × 100
formulae.example: NLW £12.21 and median hourly pay around £18.30: bite ≈ 67%, the two-thirds target.

formulae.name: Real wage growth (approximate)
formulae.formula: % change in nominal wage – CPI inflation
formulae.example: Pay rises 5% while CPI inflation is 3.5%: real wages rise by about 1.5%.

applications: National Living Wage: rose to £12.21 an hour in April 2025 (a 6.7% increase) and £12.71 in April 2026 for workers aged 21 and over. Low Pay Commission research found that large real increases since 2016 caused little measurable job loss, but employers in hospitality and retail warned that the combination with higher employer NICs in 2025 reduced hiring.

Public-sector strikes 2022–24: after years of real-terms pay cuts and high inflation, nurses, resident doctors, teachers and rail workers took strike action. Pay review bodies recommended above-inflation awards in 2023 and 2024, showing how bilateral bargaining with a monopsony employer determines public-sector wages.
Gender pay gap: about 7% for full-time employees in 2024 (higher across all employees). Employers with 250 or more staff must publish their gap, increasing transparency and pressure to close it.

Football: Premier League wages rose with broadcasting revenue because elite players have very inelastic supply; most of their earnings are economic rent, since their transfer earnings outside football are far lower.

Globally, Germany introduced a national minimum wage only in 2015 (previously relying on sector-level union agreements), and studies found little employment loss; in contrast, some US states have set high minimum wages, providing evidence on how far minimum wages can rise before employment falls.
evaluation: Market structure matters: a minimum wage reduces employment in a competitive market but can raise it under monopsony, so the effect depends on employers' wage-setting power in each sector.
Level and bite: the employment effect depends on how high the minimum wage is relative to median pay and to workers' MRP; small increases may have negligible effects, large ones may cost jobs.
Elasticity of demand for labour: job losses are larger where labour is easily automated, a high share of costs, or producing price-elastic products.
Dynamic effects: higher pay can raise productivity through motivation, lower turnover and investment, shifting MRP right and reducing job losses over time.
Union effects depend on context: they may raise members' wages at the expense of jobs in competitive markets, but counter monopsony power and improve conditions in others.
Targeting: minimum wages help low-paid workers but are a blunt tool against household poverty, which also depends on hours, household size and benefits.
Public-sector pay restraint saves money in the short run but can create shortages and lower service quality in the long run.
misconceptions: Assuming a minimum wage always causes unemployment. That is the prediction of the competitive model only; under monopsony it can raise employment.
Thinking wage differentials always reflect discrimination. Many reflect differences in skills, productivity, conditions and supply, though discrimination is one cause.
Drawing a minimum wage below the equilibrium wage and claiming it has an effect. A minimum wage below equilibrium is not binding.
Assuming unions always raise wages without cost. In competitive markets, higher union wages can reduce employment.
exam_tips: For any minimum wage question, draw both the competitive and the monopsony diagram and use them to structure analysis and evaluation.
Use the bite (NLW as a share of median earnings) and real data from the Low Pay Commission to support evaluation.
When explaining wage differentials, separate market forces (MRP, supply elasticity) from imperfections (monopsony, unions, discrimination, government).
In 25-mark essays on government intervention in labour markets, consider workers, firms, consumers and government finances as separate stakeholders.

model_answer.question: Evaluate the economic effects of large increases in the National Living Wage. (25 marks)
model_answer.answer:
The National Living Wage (NLW) is the legal minimum hourly wage for workers aged 21 and over in the UK. It has risen much faster than average earnings since 2016, reaching two-thirds of median hourly earnings in 2024, and was £12.71 an hour from April 2026.

The first effect is on the incomes of low-paid workers. For those who keep their jobs, a higher NLW directly increases hourly pay, reducing in-work poverty and narrowing income inequality. Because the low paid have a high marginal propensity to consume, this also raises consumer spending, especially in local economies.

However, in a competitive labour market a minimum wage above equilibrium reduces employment. Firms hire until MRP equals the wage; at the higher wage they move up their MRP curve and employ fewer workers, falling from Le to Ld. At the same time, the higher wage attracts more people into work, raising the quantity supplied to Ls. The result is excess supply of labour, or unemployment, equal to Ls – Ld. The workers most likely to lose out are those with the lowest productivity, such as young people with few qualifications, whose MRP may be below the new minimum. The size of this effect depends on the elasticity of demand for labour. In hospitality and retail, labour costs are a high share of total costs and some tasks can be automated, such as self-service checkouts and ordering kiosks, so demand is relatively elastic and job losses could be significant.

Firms may also respond in ways other than cutting jobs: reducing hours, cutting training or non-wage benefits, or raising prices. If firms pass costs on, prices of labour-intensive services rise, which could add to inflation and partly erode the real gains of low-paid workers, who are also consumers.

However, the evidence for the UK suggests these employment effects have been small. One explanation is monopsony power. Many low-paid workers have limited choice of employer within travelling distance, so employers face an upward-sloping supply of labour and pay below the competitive wage. In the monopsony model, the firm employs where MCL = MRP at L1 and pays W1 from the supply curve. A minimum wage at the competitive level makes the marginal cost of labour horizontal at the NLW, so the firm employs L2 where NLW = MRP. Both wages and employment rise. This is consistent with Low Pay Commission findings that the NLW's rise has not caused large job losses.

A second reason is that higher wages can raise productivity. Higher pay can improve motivation and reduce staff turnover, cutting recruitment and training costs, an efficiency wage effect. Firms may also invest in capital and training to raise output per worker. If productivity rises, the MRP curve shifts right, reducing or eliminating any job losses over time.

There are also effects on government finances. Higher wages raise income tax and National Insurance receipts and reduce spending on Universal Credit for working households. However, the government is also a major funder of low-paid work in social care, where councils buy care from private providers. A higher NLW raises the cost of care, putting pressure on local authority budgets.

The overall effect depends on several factors. First, the level of the NLW relative to productivity: modest increases are likely absorbed through lower profits, productivity gains and monopsony effects, but as the NLW rises further relative to median pay, there is a greater risk that it exceeds the MRP of more workers. Second, regional differences: one national rate has a higher bite in lower-wage regions such as the North East, where job losses are more likely than in London. Third, economic conditions: in a period of weak demand, such as 2025 when firms also faced higher employer National Insurance, firms are less able to absorb costs, so employment effects may be larger. Fourth, the time period: in the short run firms cannot easily substitute capital for labour, but over time automation becomes more attractive.

In conclusion, large NLW increases have raised the pay of low-paid workers with little evidence of significant job losses so far, which suggests monopsony power and productivity effects have outweighed the competitive model's predictions. But this does not mean increases can continue without limit. The most important factor is the bite of the NLW relative to the productivity of low-paid workers in each region and sector: as the bite rises, especially combined with other employment costs, the risk of reduced hiring grows, so further increases should be cautious and linked to evidence on employment.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: accurate NLW facts and definitions. Application: hospitality, retail, social care, regions, NICs. Analysis: both diagrams used with precise chains (competitive excess supply; monopsony MCL becoming horizontal), plus price, productivity and fiscal effects. Evaluation: elasticity, evidence, monopsony, productivity, regional bite, economic conditions and time period, ending with a clear judgement and a decisive factor. This meets Level 4 KAA and Level 3 evaluation.

title: Government intervention
overview: Markets with dominant firms can harm consumers, workers and suppliers, so governments intervene to control mergers and monopolies, regulate natural monopolies, promote competition and contestability, and protect suppliers and employees. This lesson sets out each tool, how it works in the UK (the CMA, Ofwat, Ofgem, Ofcom, the Groceries Code Adjudicator), and the economic reasoning behind it, including the merger welfare trade-off, RPI – X price caps, privatisation and nationalisation.
objectives: Explain the role of the CMA in controlling mergers, monopolies and anti-competitive practices
Use the merger trade-off diagram to weigh cost savings against market power
Explain price regulation (RPI – X and CPI – X), profit regulation, quality standards and performance targets
Explain how deregulation, competitive tendering and privatisation aim to promote competition and contestability
Explain how governments protect suppliers and employees, including restrictions on monopsony power and nationalisation

sections.heading: Why governments intervene and the UK framework
sections.body:
Government intervention in business is justified when market power leads to outcomes that harm economic welfare: higher prices, lower output and **allocative inefficiency (P > MC)**, productive and **X-inefficiency**, reduced choice and quality, exploitation of suppliers and workers through **monopsony power**, and, in natural monopolies, the impossibility of competition.

The main UK bodies are:
- **The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA)**, created in 2014 from the merger of the Office of Fair Trading and the Competition Commission. It investigates mergers, markets that are not working well, cartels and abuse of dominance, and enforces consumer protection law.
- **Sector regulators** for privatised natural monopolies and utilities: **Ofwat** (water), **Ofgem** (gas and electricity), **Ofcom** (telecoms, broadcasting and post), the **Office of Rail and Road** and the **Civil Aviation Authority**. They regulate prices, quality and investment, and share competition powers with the CMA in their sectors.
- **The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA)** for financial services.
- **The Groceries Code Adjudicator** for supermarket–supplier relationships.

The key laws are the **Competition Act 1998** (Chapter I bans anti-competitive agreements such as cartels; Chapter II bans abuse of a dominant position), the **Enterprise Act 2002** (merger control and the criminal cartel offence), and the **Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024**, which gives the CMA powers to impose conduct requirements on firms with **strategic market status** in digital markets and to fine firms directly for consumer law breaches.

Sanctions include fines of up to **10% of worldwide turnover**, director disqualification and, for cartels, criminal prosecution.

sections.heading: Control of mergers
sections.body:
Mergers can reduce competition by removing a rival, increasing concentration and making collusion easier. The CMA can investigate a merger where the target has UK turnover above a threshold (raised to £100m by the 2024 Act) or where the merged firm would have a **share of supply of 25% or more**. The test is whether the merger is expected to lead to a **substantial lessening of competition (SLC)**.

The process has two phases: an initial Phase 1 review, and if there are concerns, an in-depth Phase 2 investigation. The CMA can **clear** the merger, clear it with **remedies** (selling off parts of the business, or behavioural commitments such as price or investment guarantees), or **block** it.

**The merger trade-off.** Mergers can also bring benefits, especially **economies of scale** and **synergies**. The diagram shows a merger that lowers average costs from AC1 to AC2 but gives the merged firm market power. Before the merger, competition kept price at P1 = AC1. After it, the firm sets MR = MC and raises price to P2. Two areas must be compared:
- the **cost-saving rectangle** (AC1 – AC2) × Q2: real resources saved on the units still produced;
- the **deadweight loss triangle** between Q2 and Q1, caused by the higher price.
If the cost saving exceeds the deadweight loss, total welfare rises even though consumers pay more. Note, though, that consumers lose: consumer surplus falls, and the CMA's test focuses mainly on consumers and competition rather than total welfare.

UK examples:
- **Sainsbury's and Asda (blocked, 2019)**: the CMA expected higher prices and reduced quality in groceries and fuel.
- **Microsoft and Activision Blizzard (2023)**: initially blocked over concerns about cloud gaming, then cleared after Microsoft agreed to sell Activision's cloud streaming rights to Ubisoft.
- **Vodafone and Three (cleared with conditions, 2024)**: legally binding commitments to invest around £11bn in the 5G network and to cap some tariffs for three years.

sections.heading: Control of monopolies and anti-competitive behaviour
sections.body:
The CMA and sector regulators can act against **abuse of a dominant position** and **anti-competitive agreements**.

**Abuse of dominance** (Chapter II) includes predatory pricing, excessive pricing, refusing to supply, tying or bundling products to exclude rivals, and exclusive dealing. For example, in 2016 the CMA fined Pfizer and Flynn Pharma a combined £90m for raising the price of an anti-epilepsy drug to the NHS by up to 2,600% after debranding it; after a long appeal process the CMA re-issued its decision in 2022. Excessive pricing cases are difficult because the authority must show prices are unfair relative to costs and value.

**Cartels** (Chapter I) are prohibited. **Leniency** gives immunity to the first firm that confesses, using game theory to destabilise cartels.

**Market investigations** let the CMA examine whole markets where features (not one firm's conduct) harm consumers, and impose remedies. Examples include the **retail banking** investigation (2016), which led to **Open Banking**; **energy** (2016), which led to a prepayment meter price cap; and the investigation into **veterinary services** launched in 2024 over pricing and transparency in vet practices owned by large groups.

**Digital markets**: under the 2024 Act, the CMA designated Google's general search and the mobile platforms of Apple and Google as having **strategic market status** in 2025, allowing tailored conduct requirements, such as fair ranking and choice screens, to promote competition.

Remedies for monopolies can be **structural** (forcing a firm to sell part of its business, such as the BAA airport break-up ordered in 2009, which led to the sale of Gatwick, Stansted and Edinburgh) or **behavioural** (rules on prices, transparency or conduct).

sections.heading: Regulating prices, profits, quality and performance
sections.body:
Natural monopolies cannot be made competitive, so they are regulated.

**Price regulation: RPI – X (now usually CPI – X or CPIH – X).** The regulator caps average price increases at the rate of inflation minus X%, where X reflects the efficiency gains the firm is expected to make. If inflation is 3% and X is 1%, prices can rise by at most 2%. Because the cap is fixed for several years (usually five), any cost savings beyond X are kept as profit, giving a strong **incentive to cut costs (reduce X-inefficiency)**. A **+K** factor can be added to allow price rises to fund investment, as in water (RPI – X + K). Ofgem's **RIIO** framework (Revenue = Incentives + Innovation + Outputs) builds incentives for investment and performance into allowed revenues.

**The energy price cap**: since 2019 Ofgem has capped the unit rates and standing charges that suppliers can charge households on default tariffs, updated quarterly to reflect wholesale costs.

**Profit (rate of return) regulation** limits the return on capital a firm can earn. It is simple and prevents excessive profits, but it removes the incentive to cut costs (any savings must be handed back) and may encourage over-investment in capital to raise the allowed profit (the Averch–Johnson effect).

**Quality standards** prevent firms cutting costs by cutting quality: Ofwat sets standards for leakage and supply interruptions, and environmental regulators limit sewage discharges; Ofcom sets Royal Mail delivery targets.

**Performance targets** link rewards and penalties to outcomes, for example customer service scores, punctuality for train operators and reductions in pollution incidents. Firms that miss targets pay penalties or must refund customers.

The challenge for all regulation is **asymmetric information**: the firm knows its costs better than the regulator, which may set X too low (excess profits) or too high (under-investment).

sections.heading: Promoting competition and contestability
sections.body:
Rather than controlling firms directly, governments can make markets more competitive.

- **Deregulation**: removing legal barriers to entry. Examples include the deregulation of UK bus services outside London in 1986, the liberalisation of European aviation in the 1990s which enabled low-cost airlines, and opening postal and energy retail markets to new suppliers. Deregulation increases contestability, but must avoid removing regulations that protect safety or consumers.
- **Competitive tendering (contracting out)**: public services are put out to tender and private firms compete for the right to provide them, for example refuse collection, hospital cleaning and some NHS services. Competition **for** the market can reduce costs even when there is no competition **in** the market. The risks are lower quality and the failure of contractors, as in the collapse of Carillion in 2018.
- **Privatisation**: transferring ownership of state-owned enterprises to the private sector, such as BT (1984), British Gas (1986), water (1989), electricity (1990–91), rail (1994–97) and Royal Mail (2013). The aim is that the profit motive and shareholder pressure will remove X-inefficiency and that competition can be introduced where possible. The second diagram shows the intended effect: if costs fall from AC1 to AC2, even a profit-maximising firm reduces price from P1 to P2 and increases output.
- **Access regulation**: separating the natural-monopoly network from the competitive retail activity and forcing access on fair terms (Openreach, the electricity grid).
- **Reducing switching costs and information gaps**: Open Banking, price comparison and switching services.

These policies work best where the market is genuinely capable of competition; in natural monopolies, privatisation without strong regulation simply converts a public monopoly into a private one.

sections.heading: Protecting suppliers and employees; nationalisation
sections.body:
Government also intervenes to protect those who sell to powerful firms.

**Restrictions on monopsony power**:
- **Suppliers**: the **Groceries Supply Code of Practice**, enforced by the **Groceries Code Adjudicator** since 2013, requires large supermarkets to deal fairly with suppliers: no retrospective changes to contracts, timely payment and limits on charges for promotions. The Adjudicator found in 2016 that Tesco had seriously breached the Code by delaying payments. Similar codes now apply in parts of the agricultural supply chain such as dairy contracts.
- **Employees**: the **National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage**, employment rights and support for collective bargaining offset employers' monopsony power. A minimum wage at the competitive level can raise both pay and employment in a monopsony.

**Nationalisation** transfers private firms into public ownership. It can be used:
- to rescue firms considered too important to fail (**Northern Rock** and the bailout of **RBS** in 2008);
- when private operators fail (East Coast rail taken over as LNER in 2018, Northern in 2020);
- to pursue social objectives over profit, such as maintaining loss-making but socially valuable services, and to coordinate investment in natural monopolies.

Under the Passenger Railway Services (Public Ownership) Act 2024, rail franchises are returning to public ownership as contracts expire, starting with South Western Railway in 2025, ahead of the planned **Great British Railways**. **Great British Energy**, a publicly owned clean energy company, was established in 2025.

Arguments for nationalisation: control of natural monopolies without the need for profit-driven regulation, positive externalities, lower cost of borrowing for investment, and equity. Arguments against: weak incentives to cut costs (X-inefficiency), political interference, the burden on public finances and the absence of the discipline of the capital market.

key_terms.definition: The UK body responsible for investigating mergers, markets, cartels and abuse of dominance, and enforcing consumer protection law.
The test the CMA applies to mergers and markets: whether rivalry will be reduced enough to harm consumers through higher prices, lower quality or less innovation.
Conduct by a dominant firm that exploits customers or excludes rivals, such as predatory or excessive pricing, prohibited by Chapter II of the Competition Act 1998.
Regulation limiting a firm's average price rises to inflation minus an efficiency factor X, set for several years to encourage cost cutting.
Regulation that limits the profit a firm can earn as a percentage of its capital employed.
A regulator-set standard for outcomes such as punctuality, leakage or customer service, with penalties for failure.
Removing government rules that restrict entry or competition in a market.
Inviting private firms to bid for the right to provide a public service, so competition for the contract reduces costs.
The transfer of ownership of assets or firms from the public sector to the private sector.
The transfer of ownership of firms or industries from the private sector to the state.
A designation under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 for digital firms with substantial and entrenched market power, allowing the CMA to impose conduct requirements.
The independent body that enforces the Groceries Supply Code of Practice to protect suppliers from unfair treatment by large supermarkets.

diagrams.title: Merger trade-off: cost savings versus market power
diagrams.caption: Before the merger competition keeps price at P1 = AC1. The merged firm gains economies of scale (AC2) but uses its market power to set MR = MC, so price rises to P2. The merger raises welfare only if the cost-saving rectangle outweighs the deadweight-loss triangle.

diagrams.title: Lower costs after privatisation
diagrams.caption: If the profit motive and shareholder pressure remove X-inefficiency, costs fall from AC1 to AC2. Even a profit-maximising firm passes some of the saving on: price falls from P1 to P2 and output rises from Q1 to Q2.

formulae.name: Price cap
formulae.formula: Maximum price change = inflation (RPI or CPI) – X (+ K)
formulae.example: CPI 4%, X = 1.5%, K = 0.5%: maximum price rise = 4 – 1.5 + 0.5 = 3%.

formulae.name: Merger welfare trade-off
formulae.formula: Net welfare change = cost saving (AC1 – AC2) × Q2 – deadweight loss
formulae.example: AC falls from £4 to £2.50 on 4,060 units: saving ≈ £6,090. DWL = ½ × (5.75 – 4) × (6,250 – 4,060) ≈ £1,914. Net gain ≈ £4,180, although consumers lose from the price rise to £5.75.

applications: Mergers: the CMA blocked the Sainsbury's–Asda merger in 2019, cleared Microsoft–Activision in 2023 only after cloud gaming rights were sold to Ubisoft, and cleared Vodafone–Three in 2024 with legally binding commitments to invest around £11bn in 5G.

Energy price cap: since January 2019 Ofgem has capped default tariffs. When wholesale gas prices surged in 2022 the cap rose sharply and the government introduced the Energy Price Guarantee to limit typical bills, showing how regulation interacts with fiscal policy in a crisis.

Water regulation: Ofwat's 2024 price review allowed average bills in England and Wales to rise by roughly a third over 2025–30 to fund investment, particularly in reducing sewage discharges. In 2025 the government announced that Ofwat would be replaced by a new single water regulator after an independent review criticised the regulatory system.

Digital markets: in 2025 the CMA used its new powers to designate Google search and Apple's and Google's mobile platforms as having strategic market status, allowing conduct requirements to open these markets to rivals.

Rail: after franchise failures, LNER (2018) and Northern (2020) were taken into public operation, and from 2025 further operators began to return to public ownership under the 2024 Act; this reverses part of the 1990s privatisation.

Globally, the European Commission fined Google over €4bn in 2018 for abuse of dominance through Android, and US authorities have brought antitrust cases against Google and other large tech firms, showing a shift towards tougher competition enforcement in digital markets.
evaluation: Merger control involves a trade-off between static losses (higher prices, deadweight loss) and cost savings or dynamic gains (investment); predictions are uncertain, and remedies may not be enforced effectively.
Information asymmetry limits regulation: firms know their costs better than regulators, so X may be set too low (excess profit) or too high (under-investment).

Price caps encourage efficiency but can lead to quality cuts or under-investment unless backed by quality standards and performance targets; rate-of-return regulation protects investment but weakens cost incentives.
Regulatory capture: regulators may come to favour the firms they regulate, as critics argued about water regulation, reducing the effectiveness of intervention.

Privatisation's success depends on whether competition is introduced: it worked better in telecoms and energy supply, where competition was possible, than in water and rail, where natural monopoly remains.
Nationalisation can align investment with social goals but risks X-inefficiency and political interference, and adds to public sector debt.
Time lags and costs: CMA investigations can take years and impose compliance costs, while markets (especially digital ones) change quickly.
misconceptions: Thinking the CMA blocks all mergers that increase market share. It tests whether competition will be substantially lessened and often clears mergers, sometimes with remedies.
Believing an RPI – X cap means prices must fall. Prices can rise, but by less than inflation if X is positive.
Assuming privatisation automatically creates competition. Privatising a natural monopoly creates a private monopoly unless regulation or access rules are introduced.
Confusing deregulation with privatisation. Deregulation removes rules restricting entry; privatisation changes ownership.

Use the merger trade-off diagram to analyse whether a merger should be allowed, and evaluate with dynamic efficiency and the reliability of predicted cost savings.
Show RPI – X calculations clearly and explain why the cap creates incentives to cut costs.
Bring in recent UK cases (Sainsbury's–Asda, Vodafone–Three, water regulation, energy price cap) for application marks, and use regulatory capture and asymmetric information for evaluation.

model_answer.question: Evaluate whether competition authorities such as the CMA should block mergers that would create a firm with a large market share. (15 marks)
model_answer.answer:
A merger is the joining of two firms into one. In the UK, the CMA can investigate a merger if the combined firm would have a share of supply of 25% or more, or if the target's UK turnover is large, and it can block mergers expected to cause a substantial lessening of competition.

The case for blocking such mergers is that they increase market power. A horizontal merger removes a rival, raising concentration. With fewer competitors, the merged firm faces a less elastic demand curve and can raise price above marginal cost. Using the merger trade-off diagram, before the merger competition kept price at P1 = AC1; after it, the firm sets MR = MC and raises price to P2, reducing output from Q1 to Q2. Consumers lose surplus and there is a deadweight loss, so the outcome is allocatively inefficient. Fewer firms also make collusion easier: in an oligopoly with three rather than four firms, monitoring and punishing cheating is simpler. And with less competitive pressure, X-inefficiency may rise. The CMA blocked the Sainsbury's–Asda merger in 2019 because it expected higher prices and lower quality in groceries and fuel.

However, a large market share does not necessarily mean consumers will be harmed. Mergers can generate economies of scale. On the diagram, if the merger lowers average costs from AC1 to AC2, there is a cost-saving rectangle on all output still produced. If this saving is larger than the deadweight loss triangle, total welfare rises. Where cost savings are large and passed on, prices could even fall. The question is whether the savings are real: firms have an incentive to overstate them, and the CMA cannot easily verify them in advance.

Mergers may also raise dynamic efficiency. A larger firm with higher profits may invest more. The CMA cleared the Vodafone–Three merger in 2024, despite reducing the number of mobile networks from four to three, because the firms made binding commitments to invest around £11bn in 5G, which neither could afford alone. This suggests that blocking the merger could have harmed consumers in the long run through poorer networks.

The effect also depends on contestability and international competition. If barriers to entry are low, a merged firm cannot raise prices without attracting entrants, so its market share overstates its power. And in global markets, a large UK firm may still face strong overseas rivals.

Finally, there are alternatives to blocking. The CMA can require structural remedies, such as selling stores in local areas where competition would be lost, or behavioural remedies, such as price caps or investment commitments. These can retain the benefits while limiting harm, although behavioural remedies are harder to enforce.

Overall, the CMA should not block every merger that creates a large market share, because market share alone is not proof of harm. It should block mergers where barriers to entry are high, cost savings are unlikely to be passed on and remedies cannot address the loss of competition, as in Sainsbury's–Asda. Where there are credible efficiency gains or investment commitments and the market remains contestable, clearance with conditions is likely to serve consumers better. The deciding factor is whether the predicted gains are verifiable and enforceable.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: precise description of CMA thresholds and the SLC test. Application: Sainsbury's–Asda and Vodafone–Three used to support opposite sides. Analysis: the merger trade-off diagram used fully (price rise, DWL, cost-saving rectangle), plus collusion and X-inefficiency. Evaluation: economies of scale, dynamic efficiency, contestability, remedies, and a conditional judgement identifying verifiability of gains as the key factor.

title: Impact of government intervention
overview: Knowing the tools of intervention (3.6.1) is not enough: Edexcel asks you to judge their impact on prices, profit, efficiency, quality and choice, and to explain why intervention can fail, especially through regulatory capture and asymmetric information. This lesson gives the analysis and the evidence from UK water, energy, telecoms, rail and competition cases needed for top-band evaluation in 15- and 25-mark questions.
objectives: Analyse the impact of price caps and other regulation on prices and output using diagrams
Evaluate the impact of intervention on profit, efficiency (static and dynamic), quality and choice
Explain regulatory capture and asymmetric information as limits to intervention
Explain other sources of government failure in competition and regulatory policy
Reach supported judgements on whether intervention has improved outcomes in specific UK markets

sections.heading: Impact on prices
sections.body:
The most direct aim of intervention in monopoly markets is to lower prices or prevent them rising.

**Price caps on a monopolist.** The first diagram shows an unregulated monopolist producing Qm where MC = MR, charging Pm. A maximum price Pmax changes the firm's revenue curves: up to the output where Pmax meets demand, the firm can sell every unit at Pmax, so **AR = MR = Pmax** (horizontal); beyond that, it must move down the original demand curve. The firm now maximises profit where MC = Pmax. If the cap is set where MC cuts demand, output rises to Qr and price falls to Pmax: **price falls and output rises**, removing the deadweight loss. This counter-intuitive result (a maximum price raising output) occurs only because the firm had market power. If the cap is set too low (below MC at the demand curve), output falls and shortages appear, as with any binding maximum price.

**Regulated natural monopolies.** The second diagram shows the choice facing a regulator. Setting P = MC maximises output (Qmc) but, because LRAC is above LRMC, the firm makes a loss equal to the shaded area and requires a subsidy. Average-cost pricing (Pac) lets the firm earn normal profit with a small deadweight loss. In practice, regulators allow revenue to cover efficient costs plus a return on capital, close to average-cost pricing.

**Evidence**:
- RPI – X regulation after privatisation brought large real price falls in telecoms and, for some years, in energy networks.
- Ofgem's default tariff cap, introduced in 2019, limited prices for customers on standard variable tariffs, who had previously paid much more than switchers. But it also reduced price differences and, combined with the 2021–22 wholesale gas price surge, contributed to the collapse of around 30 small suppliers that had priced below cost.
- Water bills fell in real terms in some price reviews, but the 2024 review allowed average bills to rise by roughly a third over 2025–30 to fund overdue investment, showing that low prices in the past may have come at the expense of investment.

sections.heading: Impact on profit and efficiency
sections.body:
**Profit.** Intervention generally reduces supernormal profit: price caps squeeze margins, merger control prevents gains in market power, and fines punish cartels. Lower monopoly profit is a transfer to consumers. But regulators must allow a **sufficient return** for investment; if allowed returns are too low, firms will not invest or will not be able to raise finance. Price caps can also leave room for large profits if X is set too low, as critics argued in the early years of water and electricity privatisation.

**Static efficiency**:
- **Allocative efficiency** improves when intervention brings price closer to MC (price caps, merger control, cartel enforcement).
- **Productive and X-efficiency** improve under price caps because firms keep cost savings until the next review. Rate-of-return regulation weakens this incentive. Privatisation was intended to remove X-inefficiency, and labour productivity rose sharply in industries such as BT and the electricity companies after privatisation, partly through large job cuts.

**Dynamic efficiency** is where intervention can backfire:
- Tight price caps can lead to **under-investment**. Water companies were criticised for paying dividends and taking on debt while under-investing in sewage and leakage infrastructure.
- Blocking mergers may prevent scale needed to fund innovation; allowing them may reduce competitive pressure to innovate. The Vodafone–Three investment commitments are an attempt to secure dynamic efficiency through regulation.
- In digital markets, the CMA's conduct requirements aim to promote dynamic efficiency by allowing new rivals to compete, but heavy rules may also discourage incumbents' investment.

The overall effect depends on the **design** of regulation: incentive-based caps with investment allowances and performance targets tend to deliver better static and dynamic outcomes than simple profit limits.

sections.heading: Impact on quality and choice
sections.body:
**Quality.** A firm facing a price cap can raise profit by cutting quality as well as cutting costs, because quality is harder to observe than price. This is why regulators combine price caps with **quality standards and performance targets**.
- In water, quality failures (sewage spills, leakage) led to record penalties and a 2025 decision to replace Ofwat with a new single regulator.
- In rail, performance targets and penalties for delays apply, but punctuality and cancellations remained problems on some routes, contributing to franchises being taken into public ownership.
- In post, Ofcom sets delivery targets for Royal Mail's universal service; Royal Mail has been fined for missing them, and in 2025 Ofcom reduced second-class delivery requirements to protect the service's financial sustainability, a trade-off between quality and cost.

**Choice.** Competition policy and deregulation aim to increase choice:
- Liberalisation of telecoms and energy retail created dozens of new suppliers and tariffs; Open Banking allowed new fintech services.
- Low-cost airlines entered after aviation liberalisation, greatly increasing route choice.
- However, choice can **fall** as a result of intervention. Ofgem's price cap left little room for cheaper fixed deals for a period after 2022, so most consumers ended up on the capped tariff; supplier failures reduced the number of firms. Blocking a merger might lead a struggling firm to exit anyway.
- Too much choice can also confuse consumers (behavioural economics), so regulators have sometimes simplified tariffs.

A strong answer recognises that price, profit, efficiency, quality and choice can conflict: a tight price cap may reduce prices today but harm quality and investment tomorrow.

sections.heading: Regulatory capture and asymmetric information
Other limits of intervention
sections.body:
Several further problems limit the effectiveness of competition and regulatory policy.

- **Time lags**: merger and market investigations often take one to two years; appeals can take longer. Digital markets may change completely in that time, so remedies arrive too late.
- **Administrative and compliance costs**: regulators cost money to run, and firms spend heavily on compliance and legal challenges, adding to costs that may be passed to consumers.
- **Uncertainty about counterfactuals**: the CMA must predict what would happen with and without a merger; predictions about cost savings, entry and innovation are inherently uncertain, so both blocking and clearing carry a risk of error.
- **Unintended consequences**: the energy price cap, combined with volatile wholesale prices, contributed to supplier failures, whose costs (over £2bn for Bulb's special administration) were ultimately borne by taxpayers and bill payers. Price caps can also become a focal point that suppliers price up to, reducing competition below the cap.
- **Political interference**: decisions on nationalisation, pricing or mergers may reflect political rather than economic objectives, for example holding down public-sector prices before elections.
- **Global firms**: national authorities have limited power over multinational tech firms; remedies need coordination across the UK, EU and US.
- **Moral hazard**: if firms expect to be rescued (banks in 2008, or a struggling water company), they may take excessive risks.

**Judging impact.** The best answers use the criteria (prices, profit, efficiency, quality, choice) and ask: compared with what? The relevant counterfactual for a natural monopoly is not perfect competition but an unregulated private monopoly or public ownership. Intervention can be judged successful if it delivers better outcomes than these alternatives at reasonable cost, even if it is imperfect.

key_terms.definition: When a regulator comes to act in the interests of the industry it regulates rather than in the interests of consumers or the public.
The situation in which the regulated firm knows more about its costs and efficiency than the regulator, making it hard to set the right price cap or targets.
Regulating firms by comparing each firm's costs and performance with others in the same industry, creating competitive pressure among regional monopolies.
When government intervention leads to a net welfare loss or a less efficient allocation of resources than without it.
A legal upper limit on the price a firm can charge; in a monopoly it can raise output if set at the level where MC meets demand.
Minimum standards of service or product quality imposed by a regulator to prevent firms cutting quality to raise profit.
What would have happened without the intervention, against which its impact is judged.
Taking greater risks because the costs of failure will be borne by others, such as the taxpayer.

diagrams.title: Price cap on a monopolist
diagrams.caption: A cap at Pmax makes the firm's MR horizontal at Pmax up to the demand curve. It now maximises profit where MC = Pmax, so price falls from Pm to Pmax and output rises from Qm to Qr: set where MC meets demand, the cap removes the deadweight loss.

diagrams.title: Regulating a natural monopoly
diagrams.caption: Forcing P = MC maximises output and allocative efficiency, but because LRAC is above LRMC the firm loses the shaded area and needs a subsidy. A regulator using average-cost pricing (Pac) lets the firm cover costs with normal profit at a small efficiency cost.

formulae.example: With CPI – 2 and inflation at 3%, prices may rise 1% nominally, a real fall of about 2% a year.
